articles.title: Clarios Announces Plans to Acquire Ecobat
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Clarios announced plans to acquire Ecobat, including the company’s three U.S. critical mineral recovery and processing facilities. Clarios manufactures low-voltage automotive batteries and advanced energy storage solutions. The proposed acquisition would preserve and strengthen domestic critical mineral processing and recovery capacity amid growing demand and supply chain concerns. By integrating these facilities into its circular supply network, Clarios aims to recover, process and return valuable materials to U.S. manufacturers.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Clarios Acquisition Includes Three U.S. Facilities

The proposed acquisition includes three critical mineral recovery facilities in City of Industry, California; Indianapolis; and Middletown, New York. The transaction also includes Ecobat’s Dallas office. Together, these facilities currently process more than 40 million batteries annually, recovering lead, tin, antimony and other materials.
The companies expect to close the transaction by early 2027, pending customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals.

“As a world leader in critical minerals processing and recovery, Clarios is uniquely positioned to strengthen this highly capable U.S. recycling operation supported by an experienced workforce,” said Clarios CEO Mark Wallace. “We see a significant opportunity to build on Ecobat’s foundation by evaluating opportunities for future investment in these operations and supporting the continued success of the business. Together, these facilities will strengthen domestic critical mineral recycling capacity, enhance supply chain security, and support the U.S. manufacturing base for years to come.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: As part of the transition, Clarios will maintain and build upon Ecobat’s environmental, health and safety practices across the acquired facilities. Following closing, Clarios will combine the best practices of both organizations. The company said this approach aligns with its commitment to responsible operations and local communities.

Clarios and Ecobat intend to work closely with employees, union representatives and regulators throughout the review and transition process. They will focus on operational continuity, environmental compliance, workforce stability and long-term investment in U.S. critical mineral processing and recovery capacity.

“I am proud of what our North American team has built. These facilities are vital to the country’s supply of recycled critical minerals, and our team has earned an industry-recognized record of safety and environmental performance,” said Tom Slabe, Ecobat president and CEO. “Clarios has made a public commitment to investing in U.S. recycling capacity, and that makes it the right owner for the next chapter. This transaction completes the strategic initiative we announced with the earlier sale of our European operations, and it delivers a strong outcome for Ecobat’s stakeholders.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Acquisition Would Expand Battery Recycling Capacity

Clarios operates closed-loop battery processing and recovery systems. The company collects used batteries, recovers critical materials and manufactures new batteries using recycled content. The proposed acquisition would strengthen Clarios’ closed-loop model, expand access to critical materials and improve domestic battery supply chain resilience.

The transaction also represents an investment in the U.S. industrial base and workforce while supporting domestic supply chain independence. Recycled lead batteries represent the country’s largest domestic source of recovered critical minerals. These include antimony, lead and tin, which support defense and advanced technology applications.
Investment Supports U.S. Manufacturing Strategy

The investment advances Clarios’ broader $6 billion U.S. Energy Manufacturing Strategy. That strategy includes a $1.9 billion commitment to strengthen domestic critical mineral recycling and processing capabilities.

The proposed acquisition would preserve existing recycling infrastructure while creating opportunities for future expansion. Clarios will continue evaluating opportunities to expand its capabilities across the United States.
Ecobat Completes Portfolio Transformation

The sale marks the final step in a portfolio transformation Ecobat began in 2025. Over approximately 16 months, the company completed 10 divestitures spanning 17 sites across six countries. These transactions included the sale of its European operations. The proposed sale of its North American platform to Clarios would conclude that transformation.

articles.title: BendPak Introduces Two Double-Wide Parking Lifts
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: BendPak announced that it’s new PL-12000KDS and PL-12000KDT double-wide parking lifts accommodate four vehicles in two parking spots. Their narrow footprints also allow facilities to accommodate more lifts. The PL-12000KDS/KDT lifts join the BendPak PL-12000 tandem lift lineup, which features the company’s patent-pending independent platform design.
BendPak Lifts Feature Independent Platforms

Traditional double-wide parking lifts require operators to remove all vehicles parked below before lowering the upper platforms. However, BendPak’s PL-12000 platforms operate independently, allowing operators to lower one platform while the other remains stationary.
That means operators must move only one vehicle to access a vehicle parked above. The platform design also provides double-car-width open front access, improving entry and exit efficiency.
With commercial and residential development costs continuing to rise, maximizing vehicle capacity within existing space can reduce costs.

“Our new PL-12000KDS and PL-12000KDT tandem parking lifts feature a narrower footprint than our original PL-12000 models for customers who want to maximize the number of lifts they can fit in their parking facility,” said Jeff Kritzer, BendPak president and CEO. “Reducing the width by 15.5 inches, from 221.5 to 206 inches, allows more vehicles to be stored in a facility without expanding the building space. When filling a warehouse, saving just a few inches per lift means 20 lifts can be installed instead of 19 or fewer — that’s space to accommodate at least four more cars.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Two Models Offer Different Platform Dimensions

The PL-12000KDS offers a maximum rise of 70 inches and short platforms. The PL-12000KDT features an extended rise of 82 inches and long platforms. Each platform supports 6,000 pounds, providing a total rated lift capacity of 12,000 pounds.
Both models accommodate commercial and residential applications. They can store cars, light trucks, motorcycles, ATVs, golf carts and other equipment.

The lifts feature heavy-duty steel construction, galvanized lifting cables and a powder-coat finish. A hydraulic drive system powers the lifts, while tandem drive cylinders and a hydraulic circuit provide equalized lifting.
Integrated safety features include automatic safety locks at multiple heights, wide baseplates for stability and built-in front wheel stops.

The double-width platforms shield lower vehicles from leaks or drips above. Lightweight aluminum center decks slide out to provide open-center access to raised vehicles, supporting service and parking applications.
BendPak provides a five-year warranty for both the PL-12000KDS and PL-12000KDT.

articles.title: Think Twice Before Erasing Trouble Codes
articles.author: Counterman Staff

paras.en: Counter pros should avoid erasing diagnostic trouble codes when customers request it. Clearing codes without fixing the underlying problem will only temporarily turn off the check engine light.

Erasing codes also deletes valuable freeze-frame data that technicians need for accurate diagnosis. Additionally, clearing codes resets emissions readiness monitors, potentially affecting vehicle emissions testing.
This video is sponsored by The Pronto Network.

articles.title: Standard Motor Products Expands Climate Control Portfolio
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: Standard Motor Products, Inc. (SMP), through its Temperature Control Division and flagship Four Seasons brand, has introduced a comprehensive line of A/C condensers engineered to meet OE performance specifications across a broad range of foreign name plate and domestic vehicles, the company said.

The new line is backed by more than 100 years of experience serving the automotive aftermarket. Engineered to OE dimensional fit and thermal performance specifications, Four Seasons A/C condensers deliver the quality and reliability professional technicians expect while helping distributors and repair facilities simplify inventory management, SMP said.

Each condenser is manufactured as a direct-fit replacement with OE-style construction and cooling capacity to support proper system performance and efficient installation. Units include the required sealing components for a complete, leak-free installation and are packaged to protect critical heat-exchanger fins and connections during shipping and handling.

With the addition of A/C condensers, customers can source complete A/C system repair solutions from a single, trusted supplier, according to SMP. The Four Seasons climate control portfolio includes new and remanufactured compressors, evaporators, accumulators, receiver driers, expansion devices, hoses and repair kits.

“Adding premium A/C condensers to the Four Seasons portfolio reinforces our commitment to providing complete thermal management solutions for professional installers,” said Jack Ramsey, senior vice president of sales and marketing at Standard Motor Products. “With OE-engineered performance, extensive application coverage and a full range of HVAC components from a single source, we are helping distribution partners reduce complexity and giving technicians confidence in every repair.”

articles.title: Dana to Showcase Drivetrain and Sealing Technology at AAPEX
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Dana Incorporated will showcase its technologies at the Automotive Aftermarket Products Expo (AAPEX) from Nov. 3-5. Featuring the company’s Victor Reinz and Spicer brands, Dana will offer interactive displays highlighting its drivetrain and sealing technologies. Attendees can examine components, see systems in motion and explore how Dana products work together within vehicles.

“AAPEX gives us the opportunity to put our technologies directly in the hands of the people who sell, install and service them,” said Bill Nunnery, senior director, Aftermarket, Americas region at Dana Incorporated. “By inviting visitors to explore these interactive displays, we’re connecting the parts they know with the systems they support. It’s a hands-on look at the engineering expertise, product coverage and technical support behind our brands.”
Dana to Feature Hands-On Technology Displays

A light-vehicle driveline demonstrator featuring Spicer components will illustrate drivetrain operations. Visitors can use a control panel to switch between two-wheel and four-wheel drive. They can watch a rotating driveshaft transfer power through the axles to turn the wheels.

The interactive display highlights the relationship among driveshafts, universal joints and ring-and-pinion technologies. It gives attendees a closer look at Dana components typically hidden beneath a vehicle.

An engine display with exposed layers will showcase Victor Reinz sealing products and their placement between engine surfaces. Visitors can explore how these components fit within the engine assembly. Additional displays will feature light-vehicle and commercial-vehicle gaskets, ranging from original equipment designs to aftermarket repair solutions.
Engineering Expertise Across the Portfolio

articles.title: Ghostly statue of 'shrine maiden' discovered at 1,500-year-old burial mound in Japan
articles.author: Kristina Killgrove

paras.en: Archaeologists have discovered a ghostly human-shaped artifact at a fifth-century burial mound in Japan. The clay figurine's appearance suggests it represents a female shaman who once guarded a tomb.

The artifact was unearthed at the archaeological site of Nishikaminomiya, northwest of Tokyo, according to a translated statement from Japan's Gunma prefectural government. At the site, archaeologists found nearly a dozen burial mounds known as "kofun" dated to the fifth and sixth centuries.

This time period in Japanese history, which lasted from about A.D. 300 to 710, is called the Kofun period. Many tombs in this period had cylindrical clay sculptures called "haniwa" that were used as offerings to the dead and were often thought to contain the souls of the deceased.

The newly unearthed haniwa is about 16 inches (40 centimeters) tall; but only the head and torso remain, so it would have originally been a lot larger. The figurine was discovered in a moat around an enormous burial mound that measured about 145 feet (45 meters) in diameter. It's likely that the haniwa was originally placed near a boat-shaped sarcophagus archaeologists discovered in the mound and that it slipped down the hill over time to land in the moat, according to the statement.

Experts think the haniwa represents a female shaman known as a "miko," or "shrine maiden." These priestesses bridge the gap between the human and spiritual realms in the Shinto religion. During the Kofun period, miko would have performed important funeral rituals and offered spiritual guidance.

The haniwa figurine has a traditional Japanese topknot hairstyle called a "shimada," which indicates that the haniwa represents a miko, according to the statement. Both of the figurine's wrists have bracelets made from clay and red pigment. The haniwa's fingers have been carefully molded, and the figurine has a prominent nose. In addition, she wears a red sash painted on her torso and holds a rod-shaped ritual implement in her left hand.

"These details suggest that considerable care was taken in making the figure, even in features that would not be visible from a distance," representatives of the Gunma prefectural government said in the statement.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
Archaeologists discovered the haniwa this year during excavations of the main burial mound at Nishikaminomiya, but they have been working at the site since 2020.
The haniwa is currently on display at the Gunma Prefectural Archaeological Research Center's Excavation Information Museum in the city of Shibukawa.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

articles.title: Astronomers may have been wrong about what ended the 'Cosmic Dark Age'
articles.author: Ivan Farkas

paras.en: The mysterious force that cleared the cosmic fog at the dawn of the universe may not be what we thought, a new study suggests. The results hint that astronomers may need to rethink a major aspect of cosmological evolution, which led to the universe we clearly see today.

Around 400,000 years after the Big Bang, the fledgling universe finally cooled enough to form atoms — mostly hydrogen. But these neutral, non-electrically charged hydrogen atoms shrouded the cosmos in a fog that made it opaque to ultraviolet (UV) light.

Then, after the first stars flickered to life and gathered into galaxies, bursts of radiation ionized the neutral hydrogen. This turned the impenetrable fog of atoms into electrically charged protons and electrons, allowing light to pass through interstellar space unimpeded and, eventually, reach our observatories. This cosmic curtain parting is known as the Epoch of Reionization, or what a team of researchers studying it call the "last major phase transition in the universe."

"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," Cody Carr, an astronomer who focuses on galaxy evolution at the University of Michigan and first author of a new study of the epoch, said in a statement. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."
Astrophysicists previously thought that this fog-clearing effect depended on supernovas, the violently explosive deaths of stars around eight to 50 times the mass of the sun.

But in the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Astronomy, Carr and colleagues presented evidence that supernovas exerted the opposite effect, trapping the so-called Lyman continuum (LyC) photons of ionizing UV radiation that dispelled the celestial fog instead of scattering them.

"The most interesting thing about our paper is the observation that the strongest LyC emitters do not have fast galactic winds," Carr told Live Science via email. "This challenges the notion that galaxies require fast supernova-driven winds to enable LyC escape."
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The researchers used the Hubble Space Telescope to observe an analogue of the ancient universe in the local cosmos: six star-forming, wind-launching galaxies around 3.5 billion light-years away.

These compact starburst galaxies are generally smaller than 6,500 light-years in diameter and form around 10 solar masses' worth of stars per year. That star-birthing rate is several times higher than that of the Milky Way, which is up to 20 times larger.

The galaxies' spectra, or light-based fingerprints, revealed the origin, chemical composition, speed and direction of their stellar winds, which were whipped up by the radiation from their newly formed stars.

The researchers also described how these processes changed as the massive young stars evolved and died in energetic supernovas several billion years later, with the resultant galactic winds overpowering the stellar winds.
These nearby galaxies highlighted a counterintuitive two-phase process.

In the initial phase, which occurred during the first 3 million years of star formation, the newly formed massive stars' stellar winds carved through their galaxies' neutral gas and dust at nearly 2,000 miles per second (3,000 kilometers per second). This allowed LyC light to escape the galaxy and ionize the neutral gas and dust in intergalactic space.

The second phase, which emerged around 3 million years after star formation, seemed to reverse this process. As O-type stars — the hottest, bluest and most massive stars in the cosmos — lived fast and died young, their expelled stellar guts added to the opaque galactic gas and dust, churning it and loading it with mass, which created a trap for LyC light.
The oldest galaxies in this study — and, therefore, the ones with the fastest supernova-generated galactic winds — allowed the least amount of ionizing radiation to escape their environs.

"In general, our results are in disagreement with most cosmological simulations, which typically show the LyC escape fraction peaking after the launch of supernova-driven winds," Carr explained via email. In other words, supernovas didn't drive the Epoch of Reionization, but they may have dampened it. The intense light of newborn stars now seems like the most viable source of reionization.
Future research could aim to obtain additional galactic samples and higher-resolution observations across other wavelengths.

Carr, C., Cen, R., McCandliss, S., Ford, J., Saldana-Lopez, A., Scarlata, C., Huberty, M. S., Jaskot, A., Flury, S., Oey, M. S., Amorín, R. O., Borthakur, S., Haye, M., Heckman, T., Ji, Z., Komarova, L., Reste, A. L., Leclercq, F., Marques-Chaves, R., . . . Xu, X. (2026). Lyman continuum escape during the onset of galactic winds in compact starbursts. Nature Astronomy. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02999-z

Ivan is a long-time writer who loves learning about technology, history, culture, and just about every major “ology” from “anthro” to “zoo.” Ivan also dabbles in internet comedy, marketing materials, and industry insight articles. articles.title: 'Gulliver's Travels' Turns 300 This Week. Jonathan Swift's 'Profound Satire of Human Nature' Is Still Just as Bitingly Relevant

paras.en: In the spring of 1726, a mysterious cloaked figure visited a London bookseller named Benjamin Motte with a manuscript in hand.

Transcribed in unfamiliar handwriting and apparently written by one “Lemuel Gulliver,” the text was called Travels Into Several Remote Nations of the World and told the story of a wayfaring sea captain who visits distant shores—including an island called Lilliput, home to six-inch-tall people—and whose misadventures appeared to poke fun at the elaborate oddities of human nature and British societal norms.

Motte enjoyed the tale enough to pay for its rights, even without knowing the real author. On October 28, 1726, he published the two-volume novel, which was met with instant acclaim. It wasn’t long before the book’s listed author, Gulliver, was revealed to be a pseudonym for Jonathan Swift, a Dublin-born Anglican clergyman and well-known writer and essayist.

Now, three centuries after the novel now known as Gulliver’s Travels first appeared on bookseller’s shelves, the literary world is still celebrating the novel as an enduring achievement in political satire and prose. Translated into dozens of languages while never once leaving print, the novel’s portrayal of class, morality and societal divisions has proved universally time-tested.

These provocations are front and center in “Gulliver at 300,” an exhibition at Trinity College Dublin, Swift’s alma matter. The show, which is also viewable online, brings together more than 100 versions of the story, from early editions and subsequent spin-offs to the many artworks it inspired.

“We have hundreds of editions and popularizations of Gulliver’s Travels in the collection ... from the 1726 edition, right up to the 21st century,” Stephanie Breen, the exhibition’s co-curator, tells RTÉ’s Aaron McElroy. “We showcase the work of the printers, engravers and illustrators who have responded to Gulliver’s Travels over the last 300 years.”

Highlights include the only known surviving copy of an abridgement to the novel, titled The Travels of Lemuel Gulliver, printed in Dublin in 1761; several 18th-century publications, not written by Swift, that sought to expand the world of Gulliver (what might be considered fan fiction today); a comic adaptation; as well as pop-up books, ephemeral booklets and other valuable deluxe editions.

To this day, the term “Swiftian” is synonymous with bitter satire. “Upon this great foundation of misanthropy … the whole building of my Travels is erected,” Swift once penned to fellow satirist Alexander Pope, per the London Times’ John Mullan. But scholars are still debating whether the author himself viewed humanity with such pessimism, or if he augmented these feelings in his fictionalized characters.

Some scholars argue that Swift’s unstable identity as member of Ireland’s elite Protestant minority helped shape his biting view of English authority. “His unique dual perspective within the prevailing power structures of his time enabled him to grasp the folly of believing that one frame of reference is the only one possible,” Clíona Ó Gallchoir, a literary scholar at University College Cork, writes for the Conversation.
Gulliver’s Travels was the origin of several colorful words in English, including “yahoo,” meaning a crass person, and “lilliputian,” after the miniature characters of the first voyage.
The exhibition’s organizers are confident that modern-day audiences, especially younger generations, will continue to find the novel and its messages relevant.

“The first readers of Gulliver’s Travels were very taken with its satire of prominent political figures and the machinations of power, Aileen Douglas, a literature scholar at Trinity and another co-curator of “Gulliver at 300,” says in a statement.
She adds: “For readers today, fearful of being displaced by AI, Swift’s profound satire of human nature, especially pride in rationality and progress, resonates strongly.”
“Gulliver at 300” is on view at Trinity College Dublin’s Old Library and online through December 2026.

articles.title: Manga Are Black, White and Read All Over. Treasures of the Globally Popular Japanese Comic Book Medium Are on View in New York

paras.en: Manga are Japanese comic books and graphic novels. They are typically written and illustrated by a single person, known as mangaka. They are usually printed in black and white and read right-to-left. And they are incredibly popular, in Japan and beyond.

When Frederik L. Schodt, author of Manga! Manga! The World of Japanese Comics, published his book in the 1980s, “almost no one in the United States knew what manga was,” he tells the New York Times’ Shivani Vora.

Things have changed. Manga’s popularity is booming in the United States. “Today, young Americans have no problem with manga at all,” he says. “They are happy to read them Japanese-style, turning pages and viewing panels right-to-left.” More than 40 percent of Gen Z watches anime shows, which are often adaptations of manga, compared to just 25 percent who follow professional football.

Now, the illustrated medium and its most well-known mangaka are the centerpiece of a new exhibition at the Brooklyn Museum in New York. “Art of Manga” is the country’s first large-scale show to explore the art form’s evolution, individual voices and cross-cultural impact.

“The show’s focus on artists is what makes it so special. U.S. audiences almost never get a chance to see original drawings for Japanese manga, let alone such an extensive selection,” Joan Cummins, a curator at the museum, says in a statement. “The artwork offers a window into each artist’s creative process and an opportunity to focus on what distinguishes their work. Using astonishing drafting skills, these artists create whole worlds that are alternately relatable or completely fantastic.”

The 10-room exhibition, which includes more than 600 original illustrations, begins with a first-floor introduction to manga. Visitors become acquainted with the medium’s structure, history and two influential mangaka. Those are Fujio Akatsuka, the “King of Gag Manga,” who helped push the medium into absurd, comedic realms, and Tetsuya Chiba, a storytelling master who explored themes of war and peace, economic insecurity, sports and social divisions, laying the groundwork for other mangaka to do the same.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In the exhibition’s primary space, eight major mangaka, leaders of the meduim in the 20th and 21st centuries, take center stage. There are four men and four women whose manga represent different styles, traditions and publishers. Unlike their books, many of the pieces on view were never meant for public display, a behind-the-scenes view of how the mangaka work.

Several artworks on display have been loaned out of Japan for the first time ever. Among these are an unfinished, pencil-drawn self-portrait by mangaka Jiro Taniguchi and an illustration of the iconic final scene of Chiba’s Ashita no Joe, which features the protagonist boxer slumped in the corner of a ring, having just lost his title, with a slight smile on his face.
Twelve life-sized paintings by Hirohiko Araki, creator of the manga JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure, which has been serialized for nearly 40 years, ground the exhibition’s center hall.

“Araki-sensei wanted it displayed so the viewer can imagine themselves inside the JoJo landscape and with his characters able to come into our world,” Nicole Coolidge Rousmaniere, a scholar of Japanese art and culture and the exhibit’s lead curator, tells the Art Newspaper’s Tim Schneider.
In 2022, an artist bound together every page of Eiichiro Oda’s serialized manga One Piece, which has appeared every week since 1997. At 21,450 pages, it was the longest book in the world.
The show debuted last September at San Francisco’s de Young Museum and was expanded for its current run in Brooklyn.
“When I saw visitors cry in front of manga drawings at the de Young, I knew that it belonged on these walls,” Rousmaniere tells Crunchyroll’s Briana Lawrence.

“There seems to be a somewhat irrational bias towards the printed word rather than the drawn image in certain cultures, but this was not always the case historically,” she adds. “There is a wide range of manga expressions, some of it basic and some of it exquisite. But it is the pulse of visual storytelling in Japan and increasingly around the globe and deserves a seat at all museums.”
“Art of Manga” is on view at the Brooklyn Museum in New York City through January 31, 2027.

articles.title: This Rosy Stone Spotted in the Sahara Turned Out to Be a 4.1-Billion-Year-Old Meteorite From Mars, One of the Oldest Ever Found

paras.en: In 2022, a strange, rosy stone was discovered in the Sahara Desert. Now, scientists have found that the nearly two-pound object is a Martian meteorite made of rock that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. The findings, published October 29 in the journal Science, mean it’s one of the oldest known samples of Mars and can help researchers better understand what the Red Planet was like in its youth.

“We’re holding a piece of a rock that’s dated even before the oldest Earth rock—a piece of Mars that’s so ancient, it existed when life had just started on Earth,” study co-author Yang Liu, a geologist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, tells Scientific American’s Mary Randolph.

Scientists know of more than 400 Martian meteorites. These pieces were ejected from the Red Planet when impactors hit the celestial body. The debris was flung toward Earth, passed through our atmosphere without completely burning up and then landed on the planet’s surface. Previously, only two meteorites provided snapshots of a young Mars, which formed around 4.5 billion years ago: Allan Hills 84001, dated at 4.1 billion years old, and Northwest Africa 7034, which contains fragments dated at more than 4.3 billion years old.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: To figure out the age of the Sahara meteorite, called Teghaza 001, Liu and colleagues looked at the zircon crystals within it, which contain the element uranium. Researchers often date rocks by examining the decay of uranium into lead. The team also analyzed different forms of the elements rubidium and strontium in the meteorite, which yielded a similar age estimate.

Teghaza 001’s age isn’t its only special feature. Unlike the other two oldest known Martian meteorites, the rosy space rock’s composition of volcanic minerals reveals that the fragment was originally a bunch of magma. It cooled and hardened into part of Mars’ outermost layer, the crust, and was further transformed by underground water, according to chemical analyses. This evidence of the meteorite’s past interactions with water joins a growing body of research indicating that Mars—now a dry, dusty world—was once a much wetter place.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “When you add a third sample, and its geochemistry is really unique compared to the other samples that we have, it lets us see a different part of Mars’ ancient history in terms of what the mantle looked like and what the different mantle sources were on Mars,” says study co-author Alicia Cruz-Uribe, a geochemist at the University of Maine, in a statement.

Earlier this month, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency launched a spacecraft to recover samples from Phobos, one of Mars’ moons. Because Phobos may have gotten sprayed with Martian dust when impactors hit the Red Planet, researchers hope the samples contain bits of Mars.
Mars’ past watery environment is one reason that researchers think the planet could have hosted life long ago, since all known organisms need water.

“The findings lend support to the idea that early Mars had the necessary ingredients and conditions to harbor life,” study co-author Lee Saper, a geochemist at NASA’s Ames Research Center and the Bay Area Environmental Research Institute, tells Reuters’ Will Dunham. However, they “do not directly answer the question of whether there was life on Mars.”

The researchers say Teghaza 001 likely came from Mars’ Noachian southern highlands, since the meteorite’s chemical makeup matches what NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter has observed there. They’ve identified 13 possible origin locations that align with the meteorite’s composition, according to a NASA statement.

Still, there are many unanswered questions about the meteorite, Arya Udry, a planetary scientist at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, who did not participate in the study, tells Scientific American. And to really comprehend Mars’ evolutionary history, scientists are going to need more than these pieces of the Red Planet that end up on Earth by chance, she adds.
“Mars is a complex planet, and this meteorite is really cool, but we don’t know exactly where it came from, so this is really another example of why we need to bring back samples.”

articles.title: There’s a Completely New Type of Whisky. It’s French and Made in Concrete Eggs
articles.author: Jeremy White

paras.en: The vines on Bordeaux’s Right Bank next to the Dordogne were first planted by Roman troops and settlers in the first century CE. Known for Merlot-dominant blends, with its clay and limestone soils, this region of France delivers softer, fruitier wines. If you're a fan of Pomerol or St-Émilion, this is your nirvana.

It is here you will find Maison Lineti, happily shunning 2,000 years of tradition by making not wine, but whisky. French whisky. A thousand miles or so from the distilleries of Scotland and Ireland, this small company is making the spirit in a way whisky has never been made before.

Even though Maison Lineti is not making wine, it is, in what is apparently a world first, applying wine-science methods to fermentation, distillation, and maturation for its whisky. The result is a floral, fresh, mineral, and textured spirit.

After the producer hosted the prestigious World Whisky Forum in June 2025, its methods have set the industry all aflutter. Why? Not only does the product taste exceptional, Lineti's groundbreaking techniques are bringing its spirit to the bottle years faster than traditional players using traditional processes.

The masterminds behind Maison Lineti's wine-made whisky are Magali Picard, a chemical engineer who holds a doctorate in oenology from the University of Bordeaux, and her partner and cofounder, Alex Cosculluela. The company launched in 2018 with their friend Xavier Payan, who studied wine and spirits management alongside Cosculluela.

During pandemic lockdowns, while the rest of us dusted off gaming consoles or mined the more questionable parts of Netflix’s catalog, Picard sharpened her skills gained as a spirits development project manager at barrel-maker Demptos to research a more scientific approach to whisky-making—one that leaned far less heavily on barrel aging for flavor and instead looked to molecular science, sensory analysis, and copious amounts of data. At the time, Picard even posted her progress online as an open logbook of her experiments.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The conclusion Picard and Cosculluela came to after these experiments was this: a great spirit is decided at fermentation, not by age. “Whisky makers are very focused on the style of cask. It's not our vision,” says Picard.

“What we try to do is not increase the production but focus on the quality of the whisky, and more precisely on the steps before the maturation,” Picard says. “We worked on the quality of the wash—the liquid issued from the fermentation, just like in the wine industry. We worked a lot on techniques used in the wine industry. For example, the use of lactic bacteria during the fermentation, and the use of lees aging—which is a process used for champagne or Chardonnay wines to increase the rawness.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Before fermentation, organic French barley is cold-soaked to bring out its brighter notes. Then there’s a long, seven-day fermentation that builds flavor (compared with a typical two or three days for scotch). The addition of lees aging keeps the Lineti wash in contact with the fermentation process's dead yeast cells for a full two weeks to develop more floral and fruity aromas.

Picard also employs malolactic fermentation, a secondary winemaking process where lactic acid bacteria convert sharp, tart malic acids into softer, creamier lactic acids. Such a process wouldn't be allowed in scotch production, which is strictly regulated, but EU law permits such manipulation. In wine, the process would result in a softer texture, but in Lineti's whisky, along with that creamier mouthfeel, it adds length and even more floral notes.

Maison Lineti’s wine-based, science-laden fermentation process happens in the “egg box”—a remarkable space housing seven giant concrete, egg-shaped fermenters that reach to the ceiling. Cosculluela says the concrete allows for precise temperature control, as the material much thicker than the stainless steel that’s typically used. Additionally, the lack of internal ridges in the eggs supposedly make for better movement and churn of the liquid when the yeasts are fermenting.

The tangible gains from all this work before the fruits of their labor go into barrels are not merely limited to improved and distinctive flavor profiles. Cosculluela claims that Maison Lineti’s pre-maturation may well take weeks longer than other makers, but, crucially, it saves two to four years of barrel aging. This is how Maison Lineti’s relatively young whisky somewhat magically goes toe-to-toe with single malt scotch that is many years older. (Which it does. Take our word for it.)

It also means Cosculluela and Picard end up with more booze for their buck. A faster maturation to a minimum viable product, if you will, means the angels get to steal less of Maison Lineti’s produce. The “angel’s share” is the portion of whisky that naturally evaporates through the porous wood of the casks into the atmosphere during the spirit’s aging process. Simply put, less time in Lineti’s barrels means less whisky disappears.

“Every year you lose 2 percent of your whisky, so you need to produce approximately 20 percent more than the final volume you will need at 10 years,” Cosculluela says. “So if you work on the drinkability to get something really tasty and balanced in three years, you save a lot of raw material, a lot of space in your warehouse, and a lot of energy.”

However, for Picard, this use of these winemaking skills and methods is not enough to ensure success for Maison Linetti—comprehensive data analysis is also key. Excel files document some 10,000 lines of data per batch produced.

“On the brewing part, we collect temperature, the time, the transfer yield of the pump, the water added, everything,” Cosculluela says. “For the fermentation, we collect the time and temperature every 20 minutes. For the stills, we have the ABV, the temperature, and the speed.” As a result, Cosculluela and Picard can see the direct impacts of any changes they make. “We try to change only one parameter at a time,” Cosculluela says, so that any improvements can be tracked back to exactly what was altered.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “If we develop a project on the fermentation parts, we just need a different samples from the batch, and you can collect the data in two weeks,” says Picard. “But do a study on the maturation? That needs time. We conducted one three years ago, and we've only just begun to have the final results.”

The data science isn't the only thing that's been an arduous process for Maison Lineti. Cosculluela and Picard have been tested financially, too. In July last year, after all their hard work, experiments, and graft, the company was forced into liquidation when its main wine-producing backer withdrew from the business. However, before the worst could happen, Maison Lineti secured a new unnamed investor, a French entrepreneur who, fittingly, apparently made their fortune in the luxury industry.

This new injection of cash has resulted in, just this week, Maison Lineti's whisky going on sale to the public in the UK for the first time. The intention, Cosculluela says, is to bring the spirit to the US in 2028. The launch range consists of a core expression, called Calibre No1, sitting alongside two limited editions, named “Complications,” all three clearly referencing the luxury watchmaking world in their nomenclature.

At 47.7 percent ABV, Calibre No1 single malt is WIRED's clear favorite, and the most accessible at £50 (about $67) for 70 cl (about 23.7 fluid ounces). It’s described as the DNA of the brand—sophisticated, complex, and elegant. Complication No1 is matured in ex-bourbon casks and is limited to 850 bottles. It is more focused on the malolactic fermentation, and it proposes something different altogether, in no way trying to compete with the distilleries of Scotland or elsewhere. Complication No2 is limited to 750 bottles and is all about offering a profile defined by Oloroso sherry casks. All of these whiskies are just three and a half years old, but, quite remarkably, taste much more mature.

paras.en: Drinks writer and presenter Becky Paskin, who is also the former editor of The Spirits Business and Scotchwhisky.com, is unequivocal in her praise of what Maison Lineti has managed to achieve. “What they're doing is probably the most innovative thing to happen to whisky in decades,” Paskin says. “By leaning on their own background and oenology, they've created whisky that is completely unique … for now. Other producers around the world will look to what they're doing and potentially start to use some of these techniques.”

paras.en: As for the undeniably subtle and interesting flavors Cosculluela and Picard are managing to conjure, Paskin thinks the whiskey world is only beginning to see the distillery's potential. "You're only just starting to see the tip of what Maison Lineti is capable of. They've got all these levers they can pull. So, ultimately, we could see very creamy, very fruity whiskies. We could see whiskies that are more malty in character, but they always have this signature floral undertone. Every distillery needs a DNA, and that's what's unique to Maison Lineti.”

articles.title: Govee Christmas Lights 2 Deal: Save $25 on These Smart String Lights
articles.author: Simon Hill

paras.en: The holiday season is creeping closer, and one way to create the right atmosphere is to snag some smart string lights. They’re perfect for the tree, but you can also use them as outdoor lighting around your porch or hang them on furniture to cozy up a room. Govee offers a frankly astounding lineup of smart lighting, backed by perhaps the most feature-packed app, so it’s a great choice if you want to light up your life.

The Govee Christmas Lights 2, the budget pick in our best smart Christmas lights guide, are already relatively affordable, but a further 25 percent discount is not to be sniffed at. You can get $25 off the 66-foot length, perfect for the average tree, all the way up to $100 off the 328-foot length to cover your entire front yard. I haven’t seen them priced this low since Black Friday last year.

These string lights are IP67 rated and can withstand extreme temperatures, so you can use them just about anywhere. That said, you’ll need an outdoor outlet, and if you aim to get a good outdoor lighting display going, I recommend a weatherproof electrical box.

The string itself is green, so it blends in perfectly with a real or fake indoor Christmas tree or any real outdoor trees or shrubs. The spool makes it easy to unravel the string and get them installed. You can connect them via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi and use the Govee app, or add them to your smart home ecosystem of choice via Matter. There’s a little control unit with a power button, but you’ll want to connect them to your smart home for remote control and automatic scheduling.

While it may take you a few minutes to get your head around, I recommend using the Govee app because it is packed full of fun features. At the shallow end, you can change the color and brightness of the lights, but there’s so much more to it than that. By mapping your lights using your phone camera, you can select complex animated lighting effects. There are well over 100 presets to choose from, but you can also have the app generate effects for you based on your interests.

They may have Christmas in the name, but these string lights are so versatile that you can find effects to suit any scenario, from spooky Halloween animations to classy white light that works year-round. I've used these outdoors for a couple of years now, and they’re still going strong.

articles.title: Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims
articles.author: Lily Hay Newman, Matt Burgess

paras.en: New research shared exclusively with Kernel Panic shows that hackers have started adding AI functionality into a new strain of infostealer malware, making it possible for the system to automatically profile victims and quickly surface the highest value targets and their information. Dubbed “Volta-Autodoxer” because of how the malware refers to itself internally, the finding by Cisco Talos researchers sheds light on the ways that commercial LLMs are being used to augment and enhance the capabilities of established types of malware.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Volta is pretty mature as a stealer. It casts a pretty wide net for what it collects,” says Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos. “It compiles all of those things together, ultimately producing a serialized dossier that it can send to a couple LLM models. It’s asking the model to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured citation-backed assessment of the victim. It’s like a prioritization and analysis function.”

Talos flagged the malware using its new CAIRN framework, built to identify hacking tools that incorporate AI capabilities. Fetterman notes that Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild.

Once all of this is done, the malware feeds its findings into AI tools for analysis using OpenRouter, a service that can send prompts to multiple different AI providers. Volta defaults its requests to Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6. But apparently preparing for the possibility that the model’s guardrails could block the activity, Volta is built with fallbacks to the Chinese open weight Moonshot AI Kimi K2 and, if that fails, Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash. Building in fallbacks and relying on cost-effective, older-generation models are common techniques among attackers.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Volta’s creators included a 240-word prompt, including bullet points and a numbered list, as part of their instructions to any LLM analyzing the collected data. “You are a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment from a structured evidence bundle,” the Volta prompt says. It instructs the chatbot to produce an “executive summary” about the person, details of what they do, “what they’re worth,” and a summary of “their opsec.” It adds that the chatbot should “connect dots across fields,” for example, checking whether someone’s Wi-Fi password matches their last name. “Go deep, not wide,” the prompt says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “The prompt is pretty carefully crafted not to imply anything overtly malicious,” Fetterman says. “But they’re building in the expectation to potentially hit model refusals at first request. And so they plan for failover kind of cascading to more permissible models as they go down the chain. And there’s also the capability to still use the implant without the AI. The AI calls are kind of above and beyond, but the malware will still work without it.”

Some low-level cybercriminals and scammers have complained about AI slop filling up cybercrime forums, but security researchers are increasingly discovering other hackers using LLMs for coding tasks or analyzing troves of stolen information. Researchers at threat intelligence firm Crowdstrike, for example, recently told WIRED they had seen four distinct hacking groups with varying sophistication—operating in Chinese, Spanish and English, Indonesian, and Russian—using AI tools to compromise dozens of targets around the world, including government entities and businesses in health care, retail, and travel.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Cisco’s Fetterman says Volta contains some clues that it may have been built to sell to a range of attackers rather than being developed for one specific actor’s campaigns. And while the malware at its core is still a traditional infostealer, the AI expansion foreshadows even more invasive and sinister activity in the future.

“If you’re able to identify your high-value targets faster, you probably have a better chance of using their credentials or authenticating using stolen tokens more often than maybe you would have if you had to do that triage yourself,” Fetterman says, referencing the fact that authentication tokens expire and passwords can be changed. “We’re seeing more advanced capabilities accessible to lower-level sophistication attackers. It’s really interesting and disturbing.”

articles.title: 'General Hospital,' 'Kelly Clarkson Show' win big at Daytime Emmys

paras.en: Oct. 31 (UPI) -- General Hospital was named Best Drama and The Kelly Clarkson Show was voted Best Talk Show at the Daytime Emmy Awards ceremony at the Hollywood Palladium in Los Angeles Friday night.
Tamara Tunie from Beyond the Gates won the Best Actress in a Drama statuette, while Scott Clifton went home with the prize for Best Actor for The Bold and the Beautiful.
Beth Maitland and Roger Howarth from The Young and the Restless earned the Best Supporting Actress and Actor accolades.
Genie Francis from General Hospital was presented with the Life Achievement Award.
Sherri Shepherd was named Best Talk Show Host for Sherri.

Solo Traveling with Tracee Ellis Ross earned the honor for Best Travel and Adventure Program, Justice For The People with Judge Milian won the Emmy for Best Legal/Courtroom Series and Be My Guest with Ina Garten picked up the prize for Best Culinary Instruction Series.
Garten also won the Best Culinary Host award.

articles.title: D.C., Virginia file suit to block Trump's arch project

paras.en: Oct. 31 (UPI) -- Washington, D.C., and the commonwealth of Virginia filed a lawsuit Saturday to block construction of President Donald Trump's arch.

Several lawsuits have plagued the project already, including one filed by two Vietnam War veterans and a historian, and another filed by Arlington County, Va. The veterans' case was heard by a judge on Friday and she seemed skeptical of the federal government's arguments.

In the new case against the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior, the two plaintiffs argue that the project is "flagrantly unlawful" and that it will change the landscape of the District of Columbia forever, the Washington Post reported.

"In their rush to break ground on the Arch, Defendants have made only half-hearted gestures at complying with these requirements," the lawsuit said. "Perhaps recognizing that the project is legally indefensible, Defendants have made clear that they will attempt to outrun judicial review."

"It is entirely foreseeable that, once construction begins, Defendants will argue -- as they have done in other cases -- that an order halting construction would irreparably harm the federal government, pose security risks and impermissibly alter the status quo they have unilaterally created," the lawsuit said.

Trump's arch project is the construction of a 250-foot tall "triumphal" arch near the entrance of Arlington National Cemetery. The president has said it's to celebrate the country's 250th birthday and that it will serve as a munitions depository.
Excavation work began on the site in early September.

The plaintiffs in the new suit said they have "indisputable standing" in the case. In the veterans' case, their standing may be an issue. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan on Friday acknowledged that the veterans' standing is murky and said she would consider it over the weekend.

D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb, a Democrat, said the arch would cause "serious, immediate and irreparable harm to the District and its residents." And Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones, also a Democrat, said "Trump's illegal vanity project" would disrespect Arlington National Cemetery and the "extraordinary sacrifices it represents."

"The Commonwealth has a solemn duty and a profound interest in preserving the dignity of this sacred place," Jones said in a statement to the Post. "We will vigorously litigate to protect its sanctity and honor the legacy of those who made the ultimate sacrifice."

The two jurisdictions argue that the arch would damage the region's security and emergency preparedness, disrupt traffic and degrade the environment. They also argue that the arch would violate the Height of Buildings Act of 1910. That law caps the height of buildings in the capital at 130 feet. At 250 feet, the arch would be nearly double that.

They also argue that the arch has not been authorized by Congress and because the National Park Service didn't follow laws requiring "appropriate consultation before undertaking a project that would transform the District's physical landscape and upend its historic plan."

articles.title: French youth protests spread to Germany on Halloween

paras.en: Oct. 31 (UPI) -- Young people in France are again taking to the streets, but this time they are joined by their peers in Germany.

The German youth organization GenZ regelt [Gen Z has got this] organized protests in the major cities, including Berlin, Frankfurt, Cologne and Munich, with associated protests in 30 other German cities. They're protesting the high cost of living, underfunded schools and universities, environmental issues and a potential mandatory military service.
Police in Cologne have canceled the march because some protesters are wearing masks and throwing smoke bombs, The Guardian reported. The protesters can continue but must stay in one area.
But the youth organization has pushed back on expressed fears of violent demonstrations saying they distract from its demands.
Spokesperson Veronika Dinter told the German broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that the "narrative of violence" is causing the media "to divert attention from our core demands."

"It shows that our point about not being taken seriously or being heard is right," another organizer of the Munich protest said. "No one wants to work with us on the issues at stake but instead always put the topic of violence on the agenda."
The group planned the protest to coincide with Halloween to gain more attention and higher turnout.

"We are young people who no longer want to watch decisions being made about our future without us," GenZ regelt says on its website. The site tells protesters to remain peaceful and to not cover their faces, even in costume.
Extra police have been deployed nationwide, and high-end stores in Berlin have boarded their windows.

The precautions come in the wake of large protests over the past two weekends in France and Italy, where some rioters damaged stores, monuments and government buildings. Last weekend, protests were calmer.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk of public disorder" this weekend. He said protests would only be allowed outside of town centers.
Nuñez said some messaging surrounding protests included Halloween images calling for "revolution" and "insurrection."

"At Halloween, the rules remain the same!" the Paris police said on X. They reminded people that hiding faces in public is punishable by a $170 fine, while carrying a weapon -- even a fake one -- has a sentence of up to three years in prison and a $50,000 fine.
On Thursday, a nationwide strike is planned in France, called by the inter-union coalition over rising living costs.

articles.title: French officials eye social media’s role in promoting unrest.
articles.author: Mark Landler and Ségolène Le Stradic

paras.en: Hundreds of thousands of protesters were on the streets in cities across France again on Saturday, a now-weekly expression of national grievance that has led to clashes between protesters and the police, and kept the country on edge.

Adding to those fears: Halloween, which also falls on Saturday. The French authorities, citing calls on social media for people to revolt that encouraged them to wear masks and costumes, warned that the risk of a new outbreak of violence was high.

In Paris, tensions began flaring between protesters and the police in the late afternoon, as officers fired rounds of tear gas at people who refused to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration in the city, compared with 110,000 last Saturday. The interior ministry estimated that nationwide, 320,000 people had demonstrated, compared with 410,000 last week. Protesters and the police also clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes.

Earlier in the week, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, promised to deploy 70,000 police officers, matching the numbers on Oct. 24. That operation helped keep a lid on outbreaks of arson and looting, although then, too, there were clashes as the police tried to disperse the crowds in the evening.

There was ample fuel for a repeat of those combustible scenes. Students, who are returning to school on Monday after a two-week break, were not mollified by the government’s initial response to their demands. The Education Ministry agreed to cap some class sizes, offer low-interest loans to rebuild school buildings and phase out an unpopular online college admissions platform.

The students vowed to go on protesting. Their two-month-old movement has grown to include university students, public workers and veterans of the “yellow vest” movement that convulsed France from 2018 to 2020.
The authorities have said they are most worried about trouble breaking out after nightfall.

“We are seeing numerous calls to gather coming from the far left, the radicalized extreme left, and from certain radicalized ‘yellow vests’ websites, which are urging people to attend rallies or public gatherings starting at 8 p.m. in many cities across France,” Mr. Nuñez said at a news conference.

Some of the messages were violent, Mr. Nuñez said, calling for “revolution” and “insurrection.” Those gatherings will be forbidden, and any attempt to gather in spite of the ban will lead to arrests, he said.

Demonstrators have been encouraged on social media to turn up wearing Halloween costumes. Mr. Nuñez warned it was a criminal offense to conceal one’s face during a demonstration in which public order is disrupted.

- Far-right activists: While the government has blamed far-left activists for much of the mayhem, officials confirmed that bands of young men with links to the far right have also infiltrated the demonstrations. They use the pretext of protecting shop owners but often end up in clashes with far-left groups.
I can hear loud bangs at the end of the demonstration route and I can see many people running backward, as well as tear gas in the distance. Some protesters are throwing mortar-like fireworks.
The mood at the Paris protest has definitely changed. Though I can still hear some protesters singing, the protest has turned violent.

Police officers are now blocking many of the roads in the neighborhood at the end of the demonstration route. I saw a young woman surrounded by medics — she was bleeding from the face. I saw flames at the end of one avenue. I also saw police officers charge toward the crowd. Some residents are trying to make their way back home quickly, covering their faces to avoid tear gas.

Tensions in Paris continue to rise. Police are skirmishing with 200 to 300 rioters who have refused to disperse at the end of a rally. The Paris police said the rioters threw Molotov cocktails and fireworks at officers. A car was set afire.

Tensions are now flaring between protesters and the police in Paris. Police are firing rounds of tear gas at people, who are refusing to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration, compared with 110,000 last Saturday.
The Interior Ministry estimated that 320,000 people took part in protests across the country today. That is somewhat fewer than last week (410,000) and the week before (550,000).

The demonstration in Paris remains peaceful, even festive. But police and protesters have clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes. Tear gas and water cannons have been deployed as the police try to disperse crowds. Violence typically breaks out at the end of these rallies, when people refuse to leave the scene.
I am walking along the authorized route for the demonstration in Paris. For the most part, the mood has been festive. Someone even dropped candy from his balcony, drawing cheers from the crowd.

After, I watched a half-dozen protesters dressed in black and wearing masks push trash bins in the middle of the crowd. One was already burning as they made their way, and they set the second on fire not far from where a police unit was stationed. Other demonstrators used water to put out the fire, causing a small clash with the ones wearing in black. “That’s no way to protest,” one of the demonstrators who put out the fire said.

The protest in Paris has a joyous and playful atmosphere. Brass bands are playing music, and many protesters have come dressed in Halloween costumes. Many said they wanted to help reverse the narrative set on Oct. 17 when riots spilled out of marches across France, leading to destruction and looting.

“I’m really worried about how the riots have been instrumentalized by the far right,” said Helen Olive, 50, who was among a group of parents who came dressed as “super parents.” “We want to turn that narrative around.”

Literature student Arthur Fleury, 20, arrived as a prisoner riding a dinosaur and wore a mask of the far-right politician Marine Le Pen. “Protests are about making demands but also having fun,” he said. “I was going for an absurd costume to capture the spirit of the movement.”

Early estimates from the French interior ministry suggest crowds are smaller today than the past two Saturdays. At 2 p.m., the ministry estimated that 15,000 people were taking part in 65 protests. That compares to 37,000 people last week at that time and 67,000 on Oct. 17. These numbers can be expected to grow as the day progresses. The ministry said it had arrested 27 people, compared with 217 by this time last Saturday. Protest organizers have yet to issue a crowd estimate; their numbers are typically far higher.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: I’m at the Place de la Bastille. It is normally a bustling square, particularly on a beautiful, sunny Saturday. Now, police officers with shields and helmets patrol in groups. A loudspeaker blares a warning that gatherings and protests are forbidden to take place here by a police decree and that anyone who breaks it will be fined 135 euros.
Union and student organizers had again hoped to start their march here today, and again it was denied by the police and moved to the eastern edge of the city.

As France prepares for another round of protests, officials have grown increasingly concerned about the role played by social media in attracting people to demonstrations and inciting them to violent behavior.
Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself.

But in an interview on YouTube, Mr. Macron said that social media platforms would be required “to remove illegal content, and to be very vigilant about the use of certain features to prevent them from being misused by people who want to engage in looting or other such activities.”

That followed a report by a left-leaning online news site that Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had sent a letter to leading telecommunications operators, asking them to be prepared to block Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram. Mr. Lecornu’s office declined to comment on the authenticity of the letter.

Of the four reported recipients, one did not respond to questions and two declined to comment. A spokesman for the fourth, Orange, the only one in which the state is a shareholder, declined to confirm that a letter was received but said that “like any other operator, we are required to comply with the obligations legally imposed on us by the competent authorities, in accordance with applicable law.”
The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month.

Now, in cities across the country, antigovernment marchers are protesting expensive living conditions, high fuel prices and conditions in schools. Using the unrest as a smoke screen for vandalism, rioters and looters have also joined in.
With the protests in their second month, the police have arrested thousands, and politicians are divided over how to respond.
Here is a breakdown of what has happened.

Soon after returning from the summer break, students at a high school in the working class Parisian suburb of Créteil staged a protest, according to videos posted to social media on Sept. 18. The high schoolers objected to inadequate resources and high workloads.

Within days, students elsewhere around Paris initiated similar demonstrations. At schools in the capital’s poorest suburbs, students blocked entrances to protest crumbling infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms and what they say are flaws in the admissions system for higher education.
By Sept. 29, the unrest had spread to around 400 schools around the country, according to rally organizers.
The union of high school students said the blockades were a protest against a “lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classrooms.”
Students barricaded the entrances to some schools with obstacles including e-bikes, while others threw projectiles and set fire to trash cans.

The French education minister, Édouard Geffray, said that some of the students’ demands were “legitimate” but condemned the confrontational nature of their protests. He said that students had chased teachers and targeted school principals with firework-launching tubes.
By the end of September, nearly 80 people had been injured, and the authorities had detained more than 440, including many minors.
University students bolster the movement

Within days, the number of schools engulfed in the protests had doubled. According to the Interior Ministry, by Oct. 2, they had spread to more than 1,000 schools across France, including 220 that were blockaded. University students also began taking part.

Around this time, the authorities said that the protests were mutating from legitimate expressions of educational grievances into something more dangerous, accusing people of shooting mortar-style fireworks, burning public buildings and looting.
By Oct. 2, nearly 400 police officers and over 230 school employees and students had been injured. The number of arrests climbed to 3,000.
The actions widened in October to encompass labor unions, parents and other activists, as different grievances converged into a mass protest.

On Oct. 6, around 256,000 people marched through Paris and 40 other French cities, according to the Interior Ministry. A union of high school students said protesters had occupied some 1,800 high schools.

The protests were mostly peaceful, but a fire was ignited in Lyon, and police officers used tear gas, including in Paris. The total number of arrested rose to 6,000, the authorities said. A major union of French judges and prosecutors and a human rights group accused the police of using disproportionate force, including against children as young as 14.

Two days later, on Oct. 8, smaller demonstrations were staged throughout the country, rallying around 71,500 people. The following week, the Interior Ministry said that 160,000 people joined marches on Oct. 13 across France.

More than half a million people joined 110 antigovernment marches throughout France on Oct. 17, according to an official estimate. A major union, the C.G.T., put the number even higher, at 800,000. Using either count, it was the largest day of protest since the demonstrations began in September.

Many of the marchers were peaceful, but some were not. Around the country, rioters vandalized around 1,500 shops, the authorities said. In Paris, where over 100,000 people marched peacefully, a few hundred rioters faced off against officers. According to the police, the rioters burned cars and smashed storefronts.
In the large town of Limoges, in central France, rioters set fire to the 19th-century City Hall. In a moment captured on video, the building’s spire collapsed in flames.

Literature student Arthur Fleury, 20, arrived as a prisoner riding a dinosaur and wore a mask of the far-right politician Marine Le Pen. “Protests are about making demands but also having fun,” he said. “I was going for an absurd costume to capture the spirit of the movement.”

Early estimates from the French interior ministry suggest crowds are smaller today than the past two Saturdays. At 2 p.m., the ministry estimated that 15,000 people were taking part in 65 protests. That compares to 37,000 people last week at that time and 67,000 on Oct. 17. These numbers can be expected to grow as the day progresses. The ministry said it had arrested 27 people, compared with 217 by this time last Saturday. Protest organizers have yet to issue a crowd estimate; their numbers are typically far higher.
