paras.en: I’m at the Place de la Bastille. It is normally a bustling square, particularly on a beautiful, sunny Saturday. Now, police officers with shields and helmets patrol in groups. A loudspeaker blares a warning that gatherings and protests are forbidden to take place here by a police decree and that anyone who breaks it will be fined 135 euros.
Union and student organizers had again hoped to start their march here today, and again it was denied by the police and moved to the eastern edge of the city.

As France prepares for another round of protests, officials have grown increasingly concerned about the role played by social media in attracting people to demonstrations and inciting them to violent behavior.
Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself.

But in an interview on YouTube, Mr. Macron said that social media platforms would be required “to remove illegal content, and to be very vigilant about the use of certain features to prevent them from being misused by people who want to engage in looting or other such activities.”

That followed a report by a left-leaning online news site that Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had sent a letter to leading telecommunications operators, asking them to be prepared to block Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram. Mr. Lecornu’s office declined to comment on the authenticity of the letter.

Of the four reported recipients, one did not respond to questions and two declined to comment. A spokesman for the fourth, Orange, the only one in which the state is a shareholder, declined to confirm that a letter was received but said that “like any other operator, we are required to comply with the obligations legally imposed on us by the competent authorities, in accordance with applicable law.”
The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month.

Now, in cities across the country, antigovernment marchers are protesting expensive living conditions, high fuel prices and conditions in schools. Using the unrest as a smoke screen for vandalism, rioters and looters have also joined in.
With the protests in their second month, the police have arrested thousands, and politicians are divided over how to respond.
Here is a breakdown of what has happened.

Soon after returning from the summer break, students at a high school in the working class Parisian suburb of Créteil staged a protest, according to videos posted to social media on Sept. 18. The high schoolers objected to inadequate resources and high workloads.

Within days, students elsewhere around Paris initiated similar demonstrations. At schools in the capital’s poorest suburbs, students blocked entrances to protest crumbling infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms and what they say are flaws in the admissions system for higher education.
By Sept. 29, the unrest had spread to around 400 schools around the country, according to rally organizers.
The union of high school students said the blockades were a protest against a “lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classrooms.”
Students barricaded the entrances to some schools with obstacles including e-bikes, while others threw projectiles and set fire to trash cans.

The French education minister, Édouard Geffray, said that some of the students’ demands were “legitimate” but condemned the confrontational nature of their protests. He said that students had chased teachers and targeted school principals with firework-launching tubes.
By the end of September, nearly 80 people had been injured, and the authorities had detained more than 440, including many minors.
University students bolster the movement

Within days, the number of schools engulfed in the protests had doubled. According to the Interior Ministry, by Oct. 2, they had spread to more than 1,000 schools across France, including 220 that were blockaded. University students also began taking part.

Around this time, the authorities said that the protests were mutating from legitimate expressions of educational grievances into something more dangerous, accusing people of shooting mortar-style fireworks, burning public buildings and looting.
By Oct. 2, nearly 400 police officers and over 230 school employees and students had been injured. The number of arrests climbed to 3,000.
The actions widened in October to encompass labor unions, parents and other activists, as different grievances converged into a mass protest.

On Oct. 6, around 256,000 people marched through Paris and 40 other French cities, according to the Interior Ministry. A union of high school students said protesters had occupied some 1,800 high schools.

The protests were mostly peaceful, but a fire was ignited in Lyon, and police officers used tear gas, including in Paris. The total number of arrested rose to 6,000, the authorities said. A major union of French judges and prosecutors and a human rights group accused the police of using disproportionate force, including against children as young as 14.

Two days later, on Oct. 8, smaller demonstrations were staged throughout the country, rallying around 71,500 people. The following week, the Interior Ministry said that 160,000 people joined marches on Oct. 13 across France.

More than half a million people joined 110 antigovernment marches throughout France on Oct. 17, according to an official estimate. A major union, the C.G.T., put the number even higher, at 800,000. Using either count, it was the largest day of protest since the demonstrations began in September.

Many of the marchers were peaceful, but some were not. Around the country, rioters vandalized around 1,500 shops, the authorities said. In Paris, where over 100,000 people marched peacefully, a few hundred rioters faced off against officers. According to the police, the rioters burned cars and smashed storefronts.
In the large town of Limoges, in central France, rioters set fire to the 19th-century City Hall. In a moment captured on video, the building’s spire collapsed in flames.

articles.title: Kelly Clarkson Wins One & Loses One at 2026 Daytime Emmys
articles.author: Paul Grein

paras.en: The Kelly Clarkson Show won outstanding daytime talk series at the 2026 Daytime Emmys on Friday (Oct. 30), though its star, Kelly Clarkson, lost outstanding daytime talk series host to Sherri Shepherd for Sherri.

Clarkson won in one or both of those categories in six of the show’s seven seasons on the air. She has won a total of nine Daytime Emmys in seven years – five in the talk series category and four for talk series host – compared to three Grammys in a recording career which has lasted more than 20 years. Clarkson wasn’t present at the ceremony, which was held at the Hollywood Palladium for the first time.

Clarkson recently made headlines for an incident at a curiosity shop in Brooklyn where she maintained that she was treated poorly. But “Birdgate” had no bearing on the outcome here. There is just one round of Daytime Emmy voting, which determines both the nominations and the eventual winner. That round closed on June 10, four months before the incident.

The Kelly Clarkson Show won four other awards this year – outstanding directing for a daytime studio non-fiction series; outstanding sound mixing and sound editing for a live daytime program; outstanding art direction/set decoration/scenic design for a daytime program; and outstanding hairstyling and makeup (in a tie with Beyond the Gates).

Those five awards made The Kelly Clarkson Show the most-awarded show of the night. It was followed by General Hospital and Beyond the Gates, with four wins each; The Young and the Restless and A Different Breed, with three wins each; and Be My Guest With Ina Garten, Long Way Home and Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade, with two wins each.

Although The Kelly Clarkson Show ended its seven-season run on Aug. 31, it will be eligible again for the Daytime Emmys that are presented in 2027. The National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences adheres to calendar-year eligibility, so the eight months the show aired in 2026 will be reflected in the Daytime Emmy nominations that are announced in 2027. (Whether a show that is off-the-air can draw enough voter support to be nominated is another question.)

Ray Chew won outstanding music direction and composition for a daytime program for Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. His award was accepted by his wife, who explained that he was busy working on Dancing With the Stars. Chew has also served in music direction capacities on American Idol, Saturday Night Live, the Emmy Awards, the BET Awards and the Grammy Awards’ Premiere Ceremony.

Keke Palmer won her first Daytime Emmy – outstanding daytime short form program as producer of Glam Through the Ages. Palmer has won two Primetime Emmys, for Keke Palmer’s Turnt Up With the Taylors and the reboot of Password.

Tracee Ellis Ross won outstanding travel and adventure program for Solo Traveling With Tracee Ellis Ross. It’s her first Emmy Award (Daytime or Primetime) following six Primetime Emmy nods for ABC’s blackish. Ross’ legendary mom, Diana Ross, has yet to win an Emmy.

Off Script With The Hollywood Reporter won outstanding arts and popular culture program, beating a pair of programs produced by their sister brand, Variety – Variety & CNN Actors on Actors and Variety Studio: Actors on Actors.

Star Jones won her first Daytime Emmy in a 35-year TV career – outstanding daytime personality – daily for Divorce Court, which she won alongside Corey Jovan. Jones thanked two late legends who she described as “her two mentors – Johnnie Cochran, who taught me about justice, and Barbara Walters, who taught me to ask the tough question.”

General Hospital won outstanding daytime drama series for the sixth consecutive year – and 19th time overall, both records. Runner-up for most total wins in the category is The Young and The Restless, with 11 wins.

Genie Francis received a lifetime achievement award to celebrate her soon-to-be 50th anniversary playing Laura Spencer on General Hospital. Her co-star on that show, Anthony Geary, the other half of the Luke & Laura storyline which took daytime drama to new heights in the early 1980s, died in December 2025. He was remembered in the In Memoriam segment alongside critic Gene Shalit and such other actors as June Lockhart and Sally Kirkland.
This is the second year in a row that the Daytime Emmys didn’t air on linear TV. Instead, the ceremony streamed live on the NATAS YouTube channel at YouTube.com/@theemmys and watch.TheEmmys.tv.

articles.title: Valentín Elizalde’s Legacy Gets a New HBO Max Docuseries & More Uplifting Moments in Latin Music
articles.author: Isabela Raygoza

paras.en: From career milestones to new music releases to major announcements and those little important moments, Billboard editors highlight uplifting moments in Latin music. Here’s what happened in the Latin music world this week.
Valentín Elizalde’s Story and Legacy to Be Revisited in New HBO Max Docuseries

HBO Max announced on Wednesday (Oct. 28) a three-part documentary series, Valentín: La muerte del Gallo de Oro, revisiting the life and 2006 killing of regional Mexican music and banda superstar Valentín Elizalde. Set to premiere Nov. 12, the series will draw on archival material and new voices to revisit questions surrounding the case and the enduring legacy of “El Gallo de Oro.”

The announcement has also raised questions about the family’s involvement: Elizalde’s daughter Valentina said publicly that the family had not known about the series and had not authorized it. The project offers a chance to revisit Elizalde’s place in música mexicana, while his family’s concerns remain an important part of the story.
Ozuna Announces One-Night Concert at Puerto Rico’s Coliseo

After wrapping his Una Aventura World Tour, Ozuna announced on Tuesday (Oct. 27) that he will return home for Sempiterno, a one-night concert at Puerto Rico’s Coliseo de Puerto Rico José Miguel Agrelot on Dec. 26. The show will celebrate his catalog of hits while offering fans a preview of his next musical chapter.

“I’ve been wanting to come back and perform for my people in Puerto Rico for a long time,” the singer said in a statement. “Performing at the Choliseo always means so much to me, and this is my way of thanking my fans for all the love and support they’ve shown me since day one.” Tickets are now on sale through Ticketera.
Becky G, Draco Rosa and Jaime Gilinski to Be Honored at Maestro Cares Gala

Becky G, Draco Rosa and Colombian business leader Jaime Gilinski will be honored at the 13th annual Maestro Cares Foundation “Changing Lives, Building Dreams” Gala on Nov. 4 at Cipriani Wall Street in New York. The foundation, co-founded by Marc Anthony and music executive Henry Cárdenas, raises funds for programs supporting children and communities across Latin America and the U.S.

Becky G will receive the Voice of Change Award for her advocacy and work supporting education, immigrant families and women and Latino communities. Rosa will receive the Courage to Care Award for his efforts to support people and families facing serious health challenges, while Gilinski will be presented with the Corporate Social Responsibility Award for his business leadership and philanthropy. Marc Anthony is set to perform at the gala.
Rosalía Honored as WSJ. Magazine’s Music Innovator, Sends Support to Spain

Rosalía was named Music Innovator at the 16th annual WSJ. Magazine Innovator Awards in New York on Thursday (Oct. 29), joining honorees across fashion, tech, literature, film, sports and comedy. During her acceptance speech, she also paused to acknowledge the deadly train crash in her native Spain and offer support to those affected.

articles.title: Deep Purple’s Ian Gillan Hospitalized Following Medical Emergency, Two Shows Postponed
articles.author: Mitchell Peters

paras.en: Deep Purple frontman Ian Gillan has been hospitalized following a medical emergency, forcing the legendary British rock band to postpone two concerts in Germany.

In a statement shared on Instagram Saturday (Oct. 31), Deep Purple announced “with great disappointment” that its concert at QI Arena in Leipzig that evening, as well as its upcoming performance at Sporthalle Hamburg, had been postponed.

“This comes as a result of a medical emergency involving Ian Gillan, which has resulted in his current hospitalisation,” wrote the band, which also features guitarist Simon McBride, bassist Roger Glover, drummer Ian Paice and keyboardist Don Airey.
Deep Purple did not provide further details about Gillan’s condition or indicate when he might be released from the hospital.
“We understand that this announcement comes at short notice and share the disappointment of all our wonderful fans that we are unable to perform in Leipzig and Hamburg.”
The band added that it is working to find a “suitable time to reschedule” both concerts. Tickets purchased for the original dates will remain valid for the rescheduled performances.
Deep Purple has been on the road for its SPLAT! world tour since late summer, with additional dates scheduled across Europe, the United Kingdom, South America and Mexico through late December.

Gillan has served as Deep Purple’s lead vocalist during multiple stints, first joining the band in 1969. He is the voice behind some of the British rock group’s best-known hits such as “Smoke on the Water”and “Highway Star.”

Gillan’s hospitalization comes just weeks after former Deep Purple bassist and vocalist Glenn Hughes underwent 10-hour open-heart surgery. Hughes, who announced his retirement from touring earlier this year, shared an update in mid-October, saying he was recovering at home following the procedure.

articles.title: Macklemore Wraps Up Free Palestine Tour in London: “It Was More Uncomfortable for Me to Stay Silent”
articles.author: Lily Ford

paras.en: Macklemore brought the final night of his Free Palestine Tour to London on Friday, telling a U.K. audience: “I don’t believe that staying silent is brave.”
The sold-out event at the capital’s OVO Arena Wembley boasted a crowd of over 12,500 people, who cheered and screamed as the U.S. rapper spoke.

The gigs come weeks after he was removed from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour for expressing his pro-Palestine views on stage. Sheeran later said it was a promoter decision to drop Macklemore, and that venues set to host the concerts threatened to pull out if Macklemore was on the bill.

In response, Macklemore launched his own benefit concert with acts in the British capital such as Aja Monet, Cure for Paranoia, Dana Saleh, Nemahsis, Lucas Jones, Paloma Faith, Roze, Shadia Mansour and Vic Mensa. Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg was among the guest speakers, along with Hollywood superstars Mark Ruffalo, Susan Sarandon, Javier Bardem, Cynthia Nixon, as well as Melissa Barrera and Julian Casablancas, dialing in remotely.

“It was more uncomfortable for me to stay silent than to say something,” said Macklemore about the situation with Sheeran. “And I just want to say, I don’t believe that saying something is brave. I don’t believe that saying something is courageous. I believe that saying something is human. And those children in Gaza are our children. There is no separation.”

He continued: “I want to say thank you to every single soul that is in here tonight who decided to step up, leave their couch, be in community, be reminded and feel what that frequency of love feels like.” Macklemore added about the 50 members of the British House of Lords who urged the U.K. government to ban his concert: “Regardless of what the 50 Lords have to say, this is a story of equality for all human beings around this earth.”

All proceeds from the concerts in Dublin, Paris and London will go toward organizations supporting Palestinian communities through humanitarian relief, medical care, education, advocacy, policy change and community initiatives, according to the rapper’s team. Popular Irish acts Hozier and Kneecap were included on the lineup in Dublin, as was Boega, Sheeran’s backing band that pulled out of the Loop Tour in solidarity with Macklemore.

After widespread backlash, Sheeran was emotional as he addressed the controversy onstage in Philadelphia last month: “I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet,” he said. “My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone, and that matters hugely to me. […] What happened in Israel and at the Nova Music Festival on October 7th was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable, and disproportionate.”

paras.en: Sheeran told the crowd: “Honoring my commitment to my fans is also completely essential to who I am, and that is why I’m here tonight on my own and continuing my current tour.” The singer added that he was “deeply worried about the idea that venues pre-approve content for performance. […] This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world.”
According to numbers from the British Red Cross, the death toll in Gaza is over 69,000. Almost 1,200 Israelis were killed in the Oct. 7 attack in 2023.

articles.title: Binance says 90% of $6.3 billion hack losses are now covered, plans to resume withdrawals Sunday

paras.en: Binance said Saturday that it has covered up to 90% of the roughly $6.3 billion in token assets stolen from its hot wallets in a record crypto theft announced Thursday.
Binance said it will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets through market and over-the-counter channels until the covered amount reaches 100% for all tokens.
"All BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC are fully backed 100%," Binance said in a statement. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users."
The exchange said the outstanding 10% consists of tokens outside its top 10 that are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts."
Binance said it is tapping its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures insurance fund, and its corporate treasury to replenish the assets.

"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident. We will continue to demonstrate this commitment through measurable progress, transparent reporting, and concrete actions," Binance said.
Its "next milestone" will be resuming withdrawal services for users by Sunday, subject to security checks, while the exchange continues its investigation into the attack, it said.
Binance did not immediately respond to CNBC for additional details or updates on its investigation.
It still isn't clear how the attack — the largest crypto theft on record — took place.

The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.
It also wasn't clear who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits.

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said.
— CNBC's Jenny Lee, Liz Napolitano and Davis Giangiulio contributed to this report.

articles.title: OpenAI slashes funding target by $10 billion amid tech rout, FT reports

paras.en: OpenAI has slashed the target for its latest funding round by $10 billion amid a selloff in tech stocks driven by AI worries, the Financial Times reported on Friday, citing people with knowledge of the matter.
The ChatGPT maker is now seeking about $20 billion and its desired valuation has dropped to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 billion, the report said.
OpenAI set a Friday deadline for investors to commit to the funding round, but the "first close" is expected to raise less than $20 billion after some investors reduced their allocations, it added.

A consortium of UAE investors that includes state-backed technology fund MGX is expected to be the largest participant in the round, and as part of the deal, OpenAI would gain the option to lease newly developed computing capacity in the region, the newspaper added.
Venture capital firms including Founders Fund, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz are also expected to participate, according to the report.
Wealthy individuals will have the option to invest in a subsequent retail offering at a $1.25 trillion valuation, the FT added.

OpenAI, MGX, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment outside regular business hours. Founders Fund could not be reached for comment.

US tech stocks have suffered a rout amid growing worries over massive spending on AI. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index dropped 2.9% on Friday and is down 7.8% from its all-time closing high reached on October 6.

OpenAI, which is pursuing a listing in 2027, has been keen to close the funding round partly to get ahead of Anthropic's imminent listing as the two are tapping a similar investor base, Reuters has reported.

articles.title: Binance, crypto and hacks: What to know about keeping coin safe as cyber criminals advance

paras.en: For generations, most Americans have deposited their money in banks knowing that if somehow things went sideways, their funds would be covered by the full force of the government's treasury. Up to $250,000 in losses are covered through the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), born out of the ashes of the Great Depression.

Crypto investors are probably wishing for an FDIC equivalent after Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, was hacked on Oct. 29, with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. About $3 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update.

In a security update on Saturday, the exchange said it had replenished 90% of stolen assets and was committed to covering the remaining 10%. Blockchain investigators at TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked the attack to North Korea, but neither the U.S. government or Binance has publicly confirmed any source for the hack.
Understanding how crypto is protected online and what mechanisms exist to serve a role similar to insurance is increasingly important as more Americans invest in cryptocurrency.

Roughly one in five U.S. adults say they have invested in, traded, or used crypto, according to Pew Research Center, a figure that is even higher among upper income households (27%). The Securities and Exchange Commission's research from 2024 and 2025 puts that figure closer to 15%, and estimated that roughly 9% of the investing public owned crypto at the time of its survey. Its survey work indicates cryptocurrency ownership is more common for younger individuals, men, and those with higher risk tolerance, but also possessing higher financial literacy.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: While Binance was making good on its pledge in the aftermath of the hack to cover all losses with its SAFU (Secure Asset Fund for Users) and other company's funds — and that there's no evidence of a wallet private-key leak in this incident — Nikolas Behar, a cybersecurity expert and professor at the University of San Diego, said crypto investors need to understand when using crypto platforms that a pledge is just a pledge "until there's an actual payout."

If something happens to your crypto, most consumers are left to navigate a patchwork of options that vary from exchange to exchange and are often very ambiguous. Many exchanges say customers will be paid back if something goes wrong.
Josephine Wolff, professor of cybersecurity policy at The Fletcher School at Tufts University, said there "really aren't any legal protections for crypto assets equivalent to FDIC insurance."

Customers could try to sue a hacked exchange, she said, for instance by claiming it was negligent, or may recover some funds if the exchange declares bankruptcy, as happened with FTX. But "there's no guarantee of compensation," she said.

Michael Tanguma, co-founder and CEO of Onramp Bitcoin, a bitcoin financial services and custody firm, said that when an exchange is hacked, customers are usually repaid, "but only because the exchange decides to pay and has the money to do so."
"Nothing in the law requires it to," Tanguma said.

"Some stolen funds can be frozen. Tether and Circle, the companies behind the two largest dollar-backed tokens, froze billions of dollars of this week's stolen money, and law enforcement occasionally recovers assets years later," Tanguma said. But he added that bitcoin has no company behind it that can freeze it, so once it leaves your control, it is almost always gone.
Customers who lose funds individually are in a very different situation than those caught up in an exchange attack.

"When your own account is compromised, through a stolen password, a phishing link, or a hijacked phone number, the outlook is much worse," Tanguma said, noting that exchanges generally treat those losses as the customer's problem, and because crypto transactions are final once confirmed, there is no bank to call and no charge to dispute.
Tanguma said keeping coins offline can protect against the kind of attack that hit Binance, though there are other risks associated with this digital security approach.

"The stolen funds came from wallets the exchange keeps connected to the internet to process everyday withdrawals, not from its offline reserves," Tanguma said. But he added that the details of this hack point to a larger problem.

"Binance says no keys were leaked. The attackers manipulated the system that approves withdrawals, the same approach used in last year's $1.5 billion theft from Bybit, which targeted a transfer out of cold storage," Tanguma said, noting that every custody setup has a weak point, and in most of them it is a single one.

"On an exchange, that point is the company: its employees, its approval systems, its finances, and its willingness to repay you," Tanguma said. When you hold your own coins, he said, that point is you: a lost device, a backup found by the wrong person, a tampered device bought from an unofficial seller, a transaction approved under pressure, or a family unable to reach the funds after a death.
"Moving savings off an exchange trades one kind of risk for another. It does not remove risk," Tanguma said.
The chances of getting money back after a crypto hack

Sarah Downey, executive vice president and global blockchain and digital assets advisory leader at Lockton, an insurance brokerage, said other factors also come into play in determining whether you can get your crypto back, including how quickly the theft is discovered, where the funds were moved, whether the exchange or wallet provider has insurance that covers the event, and whether it holds enough reserves to repay customers.

"Some companies have set up FDIC-like insurance or other backstops, but whether these pay out depends heavily on the facts of each case. Even without insurance, many exchanges try to repay customers from their own reserves to protect both their customers and their own reputation," Downey said.

Crypto exchange reimbursements have followed other security compromises, such as after rogue overseas support agents were bribed to help scam Coinbase customers in May 2025. Bitget, another major exchange, had to tap an in-house fund to reimburse customers after a $388 million hack in September. Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said its User Protection Fund, which held more than $464 million, covered the loss. "The Protection Fund was created for moments like this and absorbed the financial impact of the incident," Chen said in a post on X at the time.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: By comparison, Binance's emergency reserve, the Secure Asset Fund for Users, or SAFU, is estimated at roughly $1 billion to $1.2 billion, and excluding the funds that were frozen, this represented about one-third of the loss. The company said it had set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds and already held more than $5 billion in corresponding token assets.
Downey said the steps to take if your crypto is hacked depend on whether investors self-custody or use a third party, such as a regulated exchange.

"If they use a third party, they should check that most funds are stored offline or protected with multi-party computation. An investor's own funds should also be stored separately from the exchange's own funds," Downey said, adding that customers should also understand how the custodian authorizes transactions and governs storage.
Ryan Reck, founder and principal of Reck Advisory, an independent cybersecurity advisory firm, points to the lack of oversight of crypto.

"Crypto has no undo button. Once a transfer confirms, there's no chargeback and no one who can reverse it," Reck said. In some cases, stolen funds can be frozen by an exchange that receives them, or by a stablecoin issuer at a specific blockchain address, but tracing the money and getting it back are two different things.

Among the common reasons investors cite for making crypto investments is diversification away from traditional assets, as well as use of crypto as a digital version of gold, investing in the decentralization of finance theme, and betting that as more institutions adopt digital currencies, that will serve as a tailwind. And there's of course also speculation. Today, there are ways to invest in crypto that don't require holding the underlying currency in a wallet, such as exchange-traded funds, including the iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), which has over $62 billion in assets, or the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC), which has over $15 billion in assets. There are also diversified crypto index ETFs holding a basket of top digital currencies, including the Bitwise 10 Crypto Index Fund (BITW) and the Grayscale CoinDesk Crypto 5 ETF (GLDC).

paras.en: For investors who want to hold crypto directly, Reck says that before trusting any platform, ask four questions:
- How much coverage exists for all customers combined?
- Do I have an enforceable right to be repaid?
"'Insured' is where the conversation starts, not proof your money is protected," Reck said.

articles.title: Boo! See the universe’s spookiest sights in time for Halloween

paras.en: As ghosts, skeletons and spiders roam the streets trick-or-treating on Halloween night, they’ll have cosmic company. Throughout outer space lie stars and galaxies that resemble creepy creatures, spooky skulls and galactic ghouls. And while there’s no candy in outer space (though there is sugar), these colorful images are a treat in and of themselves.

Skeletons and disembodied heads are a hallmark of Halloween, but this phantasmic apparition, called the exposed cranium nebula, lurks above us all year long. Its brainlike appearance stems from the different phases of star death. First, the dying star ejects a bunch of hydrogen, which forms the white outer bubble, then heavier material, which creates the orange “brain” within.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The name of this nebula sounds like the title of a scary story. Called “the Ghost of Cassiopea,” its gas and dust glows like a haunted spirit because of hydrogen interacting with ultraviolet radiation from a star in the constellation Cassiopeia the Queen. When the two mix, the gas glows red, and the blue haze comes from light reflecting off space dust.

This nebula, called the Red Spider Nebula, is scuttling around space while its central star, glowing bright red in the middle, ejects bursts of gas and dust. These filaments, made up mostly of hydrogen, form the spider’s “legs.”

We all know the stories about black cats on Halloween, but what about space cats? The Cat’s Head Nebula is a collection of gas and young stars sitting within the Carina Nebula. Although the shape will someday dissipate, for now it resembles a cat turned to the right, with a glowing red eye that’s likely a young star.

The aptly named Phantom galaxy lies 32 million light-years away in the Pisces constellation. It’s called that because it has low surface brightness and is difficult to spot—but with a head-on spiral view that resembles a portal to another dimension, it certainly lives up to its haunted name.

articles.title: How to ‘fall back’ this weekend without losing your mind

paras.en: At 2 A.M. on Sunday, most of the U.S. will set the clocks back by an hour. With the switch to standard time, we’ll get earlier sunshine and darker evenings—and an extra hour of sleep.

Research suggests standard time better aligns with our circadian rhythm, or internal clock, and reduces the risk of health complications. But changing to standard time comes with some risks, too, experts say.

Between “falling back” to standard time in November and “springing forward” to daylight saving time (DST) in March, experts say the switch to DST is the bigger disruption. In the days after the March time change, scientists have measured higher rates of lost sleep and an uptick in heart attacks. After the time change in November, however, those risks are lower.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Some research suggests rates of stroke go up around both spring and fall clock changes, although the risk of death is higher in the spring, says Beth Malow, a professor of neurology and pediatrics at Vanderbilt University.

On standard time, early risers get the benefit of a little more morning sunlight. Morning light is “one of the strongest forces” that aligns our bodies’ circadian rhythm with the outside world, Malow says. That alignment helps us wake up in the morning and drift off at night more easily.

After the fall time change, you might wake up well after the sun comes up—but that poses less of a risk than cutting off your body’s internal clock early, says Jamie Zeitzer, a professor and a sleep scientist at Stanford University. “You’re basically sleeping in,” he adds.

In fact, given the overall benefits of standard time, top medical organizations, including the American Medical Association, Sleep Research Society and American Academy of Sleep Medicine have fought efforts to make DST permanent—a frequent hobbyhorse in Congress.

A major downside to standard time, however, is less time spent outdoors. Some studies also suggest moving commuting times nearer to dusk in the fall increases the risk of vehicle collisions with deer and other wildlife, which are more active around sunset.
There are certain steps you can take to ensure a more smooth transition, experts say.

Number one, don’t go into a clock change while sleep-deprived, Malow says. And try to get as much exposure to morning light as possible throughout the season. (If you’re able to access one, a light box can be helpful for this on dark mornings in the spring.) Stay alert during dark commutes, when visibility may be limited, whether they’re on a spring morning or a fall evening, Malow adds. And if you’re consistently struggling with sleep, consider seeing a doctor.

In the fall, you may need to take extra care to get regular evening exercise in. And if you, like many Americans, aren’t getting enough shut-eye on most nights, consider using the clock change to set a new sleep habit, Malow says.

If your usual bedtime is 11 P.M., for instance, try going to bed when you’re tired instead—after the time change, that will be when the clocks read about 10 P.M.—and try to stick to the new schedule. “Take advantage of the fact that your body’s now going to be ready to go to bed earlier,” she says.
If nothing else, relish “sleeping in,” Zeitzer says. “Enjoy the extra hour of sleep.”

articles.title: How your brain can turn your own reflection into something unrecognizable

paras.en: It’s Halloween night. Someone has dared you to turn off the lights and stand in front of the mirror. The rules are simple, stare into your reflection and say her name three times.

According to the creepy urban legend, a terrifying figure will appear in the glass. Depending on which version of the story you follow, she might be a bloodied woman, a witch or a ghost seeking revenge. Sometimes, she simply appears behind you. In more sinister versions, she reaches out of the mirror.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Most of us encountered some variation of this story as children. Those brave enough to have tried it may even swear they saw a monstrous face appear in the mirror before them.

As tempting as it might be to believe that the monster you saw in mirror was something supernatural, the real explanation is perhaps even stranger. Your brain is perfectly capable of turning your own reflection into something you barely recognize.

In 2010, Italian psychologist Giovanni Caputo published a study with the intriguing title Strange-face-in-the-mirror illusion. He asked 66 volunteers to sit approximately 40 centimeters from a mirror in a dimly lit room and look at their own faces for one minute.

Around two-thirds reported significant distortions of their faces. More than a quarter described seeing an unfamiliar person, while others reported fantastical beings, animals or the faces of relatives – sometimes deceased. Some changes began after less than a minute.
The participants weren’t being asked to summon ghosts. They were simply looking at themselves. So why would something as familiar as our own face suddenly become strange?

The explanation partly lies in the 1804 work done by Swiss physician Ignaz Paul Vital Troxler who described a curious phenomenon. When we fix our gaze on one point, objects elsewhere in our visual field can gradually fade from awareness. This is now known as the Troxler effect, or Troxler fading.

This effect happens partly because sensory neurons, which detect and transmit information about what we see, adapt to relatively constant stimulation. Our visual system is particularly interested in change: movement, shifting contrast and anything that might require our attention.

Normally, we hardly notice this process. Even when we believe we’re staring steadily, our eyes make tiny movements that continually refresh visual information. But prolonged fixation can allow relatively stable features, particularly those away from the centre of our gaze, to become less distinct.

Now imagine applying this to your face. When you stare at your own eyes in a mirror, the surrounding features remain relatively stationary. The contours of your cheeks, the edges of your nose and the outline of your mouth provide a fairly constant pattern of information.

But in dim light, those features are already harder to distinguish—so the Troxler effect alone cannot explain why someone might see an entirely different face. For that, we need to consider how the brain recognizes faces.
Human beings are extraordinarily sensitive to faces. We can recognize familiar people from surprisingly little visual information and detect subtle changes in expression.

This ability involves a network of brain regions, including the fusiform face area, which responds particularly strongly to faces. Rather than analyzing every feature independently, our visual system processes the relationships between them—including the distance between the eyes, the position of the nose and the arrangement of facial features.

When you look into a mirror, your brain isn’t simply recording what is in front of you. It interprets visual information using previous experience and expectations—and there’s perhaps no face you know better than your own. But under dim lighting, the information arriving from your eyes becomes less reliable. Shadows obscure features, contrast diminishes and the relationships between parts of the face become harder to resolve.
The brain must continue interpreting this increasingly ambiguous information. Sometimes the result is a distorted version of your own face. Sometimes it resembles another person altogether.

The mechanisms behind these illusions are still under investigation. But what makes the experience disturbing is that the reflection remains recognizably human while no longer appearing to belong to you.
Long before children began summoning Bloody Mary, reflective surfaces were associated with spirits, prophecy and the dead.

The ancient practice of catoptromancy involved divination using mirrors. Related traditions of scrying involved gazing into reflective surfaces in the hope of seeing visions or messages hidden from ordinary sight.

Mirrors also acquired significance in mourning traditions. In some communities, they were covered following a death because of the belief they could trap the soul or reveal the dead. Other traditions have different explanations for covering mirrors – including setting aside concerns about personal appearance during mourning.

We cannot conclude that visual illusions gave rise to these customs. But it’s intriguing that prolonged staring, low illumination and the expectation of seeing something unusual feature in both supernatural mirror rituals and experiments producing perceptual distortions.
The Bloody Mary ritual adds another ingredient: anticipation. You expect something frightening, and that expectation may influence how you interpret ambiguous shadows and unfamiliar features.

In this way, the ritual creates the very conditions in which something unsettling might appear. The legend tells you what to expect, and your visual system may provide something that seems to confirm it. So, this Halloween, remember that you don’t need to believe in ghosts for something strange to happen.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

articles.title: A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics
articles.author: Allie Skalnik

paras.en: One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.

The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.

Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.

The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.

There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.

Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.

The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.

The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.
While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.

The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.

“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.

Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

articles.title: Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller
articles.author: Jake Buehler

paras.en: These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).
“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.
As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

paras.en: “These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

articles.title: Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course
articles.author: Anirban Mukhopadhyay

paras.en: Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.
“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

articles.title: Earth's Supposedly Impenetrable Radiation Barrier Has Been Breached
articles.author: Michelle Starr

paras.en: Looking at photographs of Earth suspended against the darkness of space, you'd be forgiven for thinking our planet is isolated and alone.

But there's more to near-Earth space than meets the eye. Our world is cozily snuggled in the Van Allen belts – two donut-shaped regions of space filled with energetic protons and electrons, confined by the planetary magnetic field.

The outer belt is populated largely by electrons energized by processes driven by the Sun, while many of the inner belt's protons originate from particles produced when cosmic rays strike Earth's atmosphere.
For more than a decade, it has been thought that this inner belt forms an impenetrable barrier to ultra-relativistic 'killer' electrons, preventing them from venturing too close to Earth.
But new evidence has emerged that, under the right set of circumstances, this region is not as secure as we thought.

During an insanely powerful solar storm that buffeted Earth in May 2024, a Japanese satellite recorded electrons in this region being accelerated to megaelectronvolt energies – in a place where scientists thought it wasn't supposed to happen.

"Here we show that this barrier can be breached under extreme space weather conditions," writes a team led by space physicist Yoshizumi Miyoshi of Nagoya University in a paper published in Geophysical Research Letters.

So-called 'killer' electrons, known for decades, are a big problem in low-Earth space. These particles can be accelerated to almost the speed of light by interactions with electromagnetic waves in Earth's magnetic environment, particularly during geomagnetic storms.

They carry so much energy that they can penetrate satellite shielding, potentially damaging sensitive electronics and shortening the lifespans of spacecraft. They're not good for humans, either, posing an elevated radiation hazard to astronauts.

But in 2014, researchers discovered something peculiar. Observations from NASA's Van Allen Probes revealed a weirdly sharp boundary, about three Earth radii from the planet's center, beyond which the most energetic electrons rarely ventured.

Scientists described this as an "impenetrable barrier," proposing that electromagnetic waves within a region of cold plasma surrounding Earth help scatter the electrons out of their trapped orbits, sending them plunging into the atmosphere. Combined with the electrons' slow inward migration, this seemed to create a natural barrier that kept them at bay.
Even as early as 2018, however, cracks began to appear in the so-called 'impenetrable' barrier.
Researchers proposed that the barrier wasn't a barrier at all, but an illusion created by the limited duration of geomagnetic storms.
Energetic electrons could be pushed inward by fluctuations in Earth's magnetic field, but the storms driving that movement typically petered out before the electrons could venture much farther.

Then, in 2024, researchers analyzing observations captured between 1996 and 2006 discovered that lightning-generated electromagnetic waves could send killer electrons already trapped in the inner radiation belt tumbling toward Earth's atmosphere.
These observations provided further evidence that megaelectronvolt electrons were already present well inside the supposedly impenetrable boundary.
But next, in May 2024, came the solar superstorm.
The Sun exploded in a series of flares and coronal mass ejections that blasted billions of tons of magnetized plasma screaming across the Solar System.
Here on Earth, the result was a level G5 geomagnetic storm – the most powerful category on the geomagnetic storm scale, so intense its effects were recorded even at the bottom of the ocean.
The storm dramatically depleted the cold plasma in Earth's plasmasphere, creating an unusually sparse environment in which a different kind of electromagnetic wave, called chorus, could thrive.
"When converted into audio, it sounds like a bird song," Miyoshi says.
And, instead of scattering the electrons away, as other waves normally do, these waves appear to have accelerated them to ludicrous energies, right inside the 'impenetrable' barrier.
The evidence came from Japan's Arase satellite, which had been monitoring the radiation belts since 2017.

During the storm's recovery phase, Arase detected a dramatic increase in ultra-relativistic electrons inside the barrier. At energies around 3 megaelectronvolts, the electron flux ballooned by more than 5,000 times compared to pre-storm levels.
The timing and evolution of that increase were particularly revealing.

Lower-energy electrons emerged in number first. Around half a day later, electrons with higher energies followed. And roughly a day after the initial increase, electrons carrying more than 3 megaelectronvolts of energy had surged in number, too.
This staggered progression suggested that the electrons weren't simply being swept inward from elsewhere. They were gaining energy right there, inside the supposedly protected region.
Miyoshi and his colleagues found further clues in the distribution of the electrons, which formed a distinct peak near the barrier's boundary.
That pattern is difficult to explain through inward transport alone, but is consistent with electrons being accelerated locally before spreading farther inward and outward.
Put together, the evidence suggests that the depletion of the cold plasma created the perfect conditions for electrons to behave in a way that is normally only seen farther from Earth.
And it took months to recover. Arase continued to observe declining levels of ultra-relativistic electrons until October 2024, when another solar storm buffeted near-Earth space.
It's a finding that hints the dynamics of the space around Earth are far more complex than its apparent serenity suggests.
"This discovery highlights the need to understand and predict how energetic electrons behave under extreme space weather conditions," Miyoshi says.
"Such knowledge is important for assessing radiation risks to spacecraft and improving future space weather predictions."
The research has been published in Geophysical Research Letters.

articles.title: Does It Matter if Men Pee Sitting or Standing? A Randomized Test Has an Answer
articles.author: Carly Cassella

paras.en: It's a question that many men may have pondered: Should they pee sitting down or standing up?
The best option may not be the same for everyone.
Past research suggests that men with enlarged prostates or other urinary issues may be better off sitting down.
Compared to standing, it's possible that sitting may relax the pelvic floor and empty the bladder more completely.
When men aged 50 or younger urinate sitting down, evidence suggests there may be a higher risk of post-urination 'dribble'.
Now, a randomized crossover trial has put the dilemma to the test.
The research was led by scientists at the Colombian Urology Research Group, and the findings are published in Neurourology and Urodynamics.
The crossover study included 52 healthy male volunteers between the ages of 18 and 39 who had their urination monitored while sitting and standing.
Roughly half the group was randomized to sit first, then stand, while the other half tried standing, then sitting.
Between each posture, participants took a break of at least 24 hours, as a 'washout period'.
During a single pee, researchers measured the maximum urine flow rate – or how fast urine comes out at its peak – as well as the total amount of urine expelled.
Sitting or standing didn't seem to change the results.
"In healthy men, voiding posture did not significantly modify the maximum urinary flow rate or voided volume," the team concluded.
The only difference was that it took healthy men ever so slightly longer to reach their fastest urine flow when standing.
The difference was statistically significant, but it partly hinged on a single outlier, and researchers say it is unlikely to be clinically meaningful.
In the end, the results of the trial suggest that for healthy men, it doesn't really matter how they go to the bathroom.
In 2023, a global survey of more than 7,000 men found that in the United States, roughly 10 percent of men sit while they pee, though the rate is much higher in other nations.
In Germany, for instance, 40 percent of men report sitting while urinating, and yet the German word for this phenomenon is still sometimes used as an insult.

The decision to sit or stand while urinating can be heavily stigmatized in some cultures, and yet based on the literature at hand, it's one that doesn't really seem to matter that much in the end, beyond issues of hygiene.

"Regardless of the position, there seems to be no difference in the time taken to pee, the flow rate, and how completely the bladder is emptied," wrote bladder physiology researchers, Christian Moro and Charlotte Phelps, for The Conversation in 2023.
"So long as there are no urinary concerns, men are free to choose their preferred position. If you choose to stand, just be sure to aim well."
If there are urinary concerns, however, the healthiest stance may differ.
A survey from 2020, for instance, found that among nearly 200 men, those who preferred to sit while peeing were more likely to report urinary tract symptoms.
This does not mean that sitting is causing the issues. Survey respondents could be choosing to sit because they are already experiencing urinary difficulties.
After the age of 50, many men develop enlarged prostates that may restrict their urethra and make it harder to pee.
Urologist Rena Malik explained on YouTube that this may cause some to strain when they urinate or deliver a weaker stream.
That can make it difficult to stand and aim.
"So sitting can be more convenient for hygiene purposes," Malik explained.
"But these are all theories," she admitted.
In 2014, a meta-analysis of 11 studies found that sitting while urinating was associated with greater bladder emptying, but only in men with lower urinary tract symptoms.
Among healthy men, there were no posture‐related differences.
The studies included in this review, however, tend to have small sample sizes and lack randomization of the standing-versus-sitting sequence.
"And, crucially," the authors of the most recent study add, "those reporting 'no differences' rarely perform formal equivalence analyses, which leads to claims that exceed what the data can support."
This new research addresses some of those limitations.
"From a clinical perspective," the authors conclude, the posture of urination "appears to have little practical influence on uroflowmetry in healthy men."
Healthy men, the team adds, can therefore "void in their preferred position".
The research has been published in Neurourology and Urodynamics.

articles.title: Interstellar Visitor 3I/ATLAS Just Got Even Weirder, And May Contain 10-Billion-Year-Old Material
articles.author: Ivan Farkas

paras.en: Exiled interstellar visitors like comet 3I/ATLAS are time capsules from the cosmos at large, yeeted from their exosolar homes by an unknown cataclysm and forced to drift through lonely space for billions of years, perhaps.
If they're lucky, they may cross paths with another star, such as the Sun, and warm themselves at our solar hearth for a short while before speeding back out into darkness.
This is lucky for us, too, since we get an unprecedented look at a chunk of an alien Solar System, which may have formed long before ours with chemistry unlike anything glimpsed before.
In fact, the exosolar system that formed 3I/ATLAS may have assembled it more than 7 billion years before our Sun ignited into life – possibly even before 3I/ATLAS's own star erupted.

In a new study in the journal Nature Astronomy, a research team led by NASA Solar System Exploration Division scientists analyzed the chemical cocktail emanating from the interstellar comet's excited atmosphere.

They used the James Webb Space Telescope's unmatched infrared capabilities to view the comet in late December 2025, when it was about 2.5 times as far from the Sun as we are, shooting through the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

At this distance, its atmosphere, or coma, starts puffing up substantially as solar radiation sublimates its icy volatile chemicals. Think of it like the comet sneezing when it sees the Sun, in an astrophysical version of the possibly fake-sounding photic sneeze reflex, which makes people sneeze in response to bright lights.

The researchers focused on its deuterium-to-hydrogen (D/H) ratio, which is highly revealing because it shows how much deuterium – a heavier version of hydrogen – an object has in proportion to the lighter, regular hydrogen.
In this instance, they checked this ratio in another molecule, methane, to see how much heavy methane the 3I/ATLAS retained since its frozen dust grains formed.

They found it held significantly more than any body in the Solar System, and 13 times more than comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, the only other local comet to display a "secure" signature, which required in-situ measurements from the Rosetta spacecraft.

"The elevated D/H ratio for methane in 3I/ATLAS is consistent with the hypothesis that its ices formed in a cold, low-metallicity interstellar or protostellar environment under a high cosmic ray irradiation rate," the researchers explain.

One possible origin is within the pancake-shaped planet-forming disk of dust and gas around a very young or forming star. These astro-environments are hard to study because they're thickly opaque, hiding the cool chemical actions occurring within, so researchers may often rely on astrochemical models.

And this is why 3I/ATLAS is so precious: it's a pristine sample ejected from the hidden depths of an ancient cosmic nursery, possibly around one of the Milky Way's oldest stars, and delivered directly to our doorstep by the caprices of gravity.
Viewing its molecular emission, akin to it losing its lunch due to the cosmic carsickness of hurtling toward the Sun, allowed astronomers to prod various pertinent puzzles.

Its isotopic ratios hint that it may have been exposed to lots of radiation. And maybe born in a prestellar core: a dense region of super-cold gas (since its interior is protected from starlight) and the earliest stages of star formation, so frigid that it acts as a cryo-preserver.

At temperatures of around -263 degrees Celsius (-440 degrees Fahrenheit), gases freeze onto dust grains, favoring deuterium since it's heavier than hydrogen, and producing distinctive D/H ratios in molecules like methane.

Additionally, low carbon-13 content of 3I/ATLAS suggests its incredible age, originating in an ancient Universe that had not yet been enriched by generations of stars fusing heavier elements and releasing them space-ward during their explosive supernova deaths.

So, overall, this work highlights the mind-boggling extent of cosmic timelines. This comet from who knows where could have been traveling for 7 billion years before our Solar System existed. It may have formed before many of the atoms that comprise our Sun and planets were even forged in the hearts of massive stars, which died (and left behind remnants, of course) to seed our existence.
The research has been published in Nature Astronomy.

articles.title: Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424°F

paras.en: Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424Â°F

- Scientists have discovered a surprising mechanism that allows certain metals to resist cracking at temperatures as low as -253Â°C (-424Â°F), when similar materials typically become dangerously brittle. Instead of breaking, two experimental alloys reorganize their internal structures, creating new ways to absorb stress and remain flexible.

Scientists have uncovered an unexpected way certain metals can withstand extreme cold without becoming dangerously brittle. The discovery challenges long-standing ideas about how metals behave at extremely low temperatures and could help engineers develop tougher materials for some of the harshest environments imaginable.

The findings, published October 14 in Nature, reveal a previously unknown microscopic process that allows two experimental metal alloys to remain remarkably resistant to damage at just 20 kelvin, or -253°C (-424°F). The research was led by an international team from the University of California, Berkeley, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the University of Oxford.
Why Extreme Cold Makes Some Metals Brittle

Cooling a metal generally increases its strength, but this improvement can come with a serious drawback. Certain metals become increasingly brittle as temperatures fall, making them more likely to crack or break instead of bending under pressure.

This problem is particularly important for a family of materials known as body-centered cubic metals (such as iron, tungsten, and chromium). Their atoms are arranged in a specific crystal pattern that can make them especially vulnerable to brittle failure in extreme cold. At temperatures approaching absolute zero, a small crack that might ordinarily be accommodated by the metal changing shape can instead spread and cause a fracture.

However, researchers discovered that two experimental alloys made from niobium and titanium behave very differently. Even when cooled to -253°C, both materials maintained an impressive ability to withstand damage. Neither showed a measurable shift toward brittle behavior at the lowest temperature tested.

The explanation lies in a surprising change in how the metals respond to stress. Rather than relying on their usual method of deformation, the alloys activate a different microscopic process that helps prevent cracks from spreading.
A Hidden Mechanism Helps Metals Resist Cracking

Under normal conditions, body-centered cubic metals bend and change shape through the movement of tiny defects within their crystal structures. These defects, called dislocations, allow layers of atoms to shift relative to one another, helping the material absorb stress without breaking.

As temperatures drop, however, these dislocations become increasingly difficult to move. With fewer ways to accommodate the forces concentrated around a crack, the metal becomes more likely to fracture.
The newly studied alloys have another way to respond.

Researchers observed a process called nanoscale 'twinning', in which tiny sections of the metal's crystal structure rearrange into mirror-image patterns. This occurs alongside a localized change in the crystal structure itself.

When these newly formed regions encounter the boundaries separating neighboring crystals, they produce concentrated areas of stress. Those stress concentrations generate additional defects, giving the metal new opportunities to deform rather than crack.

The researchers compare this behavior to a road system finding alternative routes when its usual roads become blocked by ice. As extreme cold makes conventional deformation increasingly difficult, the newly formed crystal structures provide other pathways for the metal to accommodate stress.
By creating these new pathways, the material can continue absorbing forces around potential fractures instead of failing abruptly.
A Breakthrough for Metals Used in Extreme Environments

The findings suggest a new approach to developing structural metals that can withstand exceptionally low temperatures. Such materials could be valuable in energy systems, transportation, and aerospace engineering, where components may encounter severe thermal conditions.

Oxford corresponding author Professor Dong Liu (Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford) said: "For decades, the ductile-to-brittle transition has been viewed as a fundamental limitation of body-centered cubic metals. What surprised us is that these alloys remain remarkably damage tolerant even at 20 kelvin. By uncovering how twinning and phase transformation work together to generate plasticity before conventional dislocation motion, we identified a new pathway for designing structural body-centered cubic metals that can operate in extreme cryogenic environments. This class of materials will be extremely useful for components experiencing extreme hot and cold temperatures in one application."

paras.en: The discovery also changes how scientists may need to think about what determines whether a metal becomes brittle. Previously, much of the emphasis was placed on how easily existing defects could travel through a material. The new results indicate that generating fresh defects may be just as important.

Lead author Dr. David Cook (University of California, Berkeley at the time of the study, now University of Cambridge) said: "Our results suggest we should change how we think about what governs the transition to brittleness for these metals. Traditionally, the focus was on how readily existing dislocations can move through a metal, but now it appears that the ability to create new dislocations at interfaces may also be critical. Using these insights, we may be able to design underlying microstructural conditions that allow a material to create its own routes to remain ductile at extreme temperatures."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: To investigate how the alloys performed under such punishing conditions, the team conducted experiments using the Engin-X instrument at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source in Oxfordshire.

The researchers used gaseous helium to cool metal samples to approximately -253°C. While directing a beam of neutrons through the materials, they used a specialized testing machine to stretch the samples by pulling from opposite ends.

This setup allowed the team to measure the forces the metals could withstand and determine how far they could stretch before breaking. The neutron measurements also helped researchers investigate what was happening inside the materials as they were deformed.

Afterward, the scientists examined the tested samples using powerful electron microscopes. These instruments revealed extremely small structural changes within the metal, including those near cracks that helped explain its unusual resistance to damage.

The team also used atom-probe analysis to determine how individual elements were distributed throughout the alloys. Combined with computer modeling, these measurements helped establish how the different microscopic processes worked together to prevent brittle failure.

The results offer more than an explanation for the surprising behavior of two experimental alloys. They identify a potentially useful strategy for designing metals that can remain tough even when conventional methods of deformation stop working, opening new possibilities for technologies that must operate in extreme cold.

The international collaboration included researchers from the University of California, Berkeley; Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory; the University of Oxford; the University of Bristol; the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source, Science and Technology Facilities Council; the University of California, Irvine; Pacific Northwest National Laboratory; Texas A&M University; and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.
